# About tarot and Taro

Taro is a reflective tarot journal. It uses the images and traditions of tarot as prompts for thinking about your life, your choices and your feelings. It does not predict the future, and nothing in the app tells you what is going to happen.

## A short history of tarot

Tarot began as a deck of playing cards. The earliest known decks were painted in northern Italy in the fifteenth century for a card game, and some of those games are still played in parts of Europe today. A tarot deck has four suits, like ordinary playing cards, plus a set of picture cards called trumps.

In the late eighteenth century, writers in France began to treat the cards as a source of symbolism and meaning rather than only as a game. Over the following century, many authors added their own ideas, and in the early twentieth century an influential English deck gave every card, including the numbered ones, an illustrated scene. Most modern decks, and the traditional card names used in Taro, follow that structure.

Today people use tarot in many ways: as art, as a creative tool, as a game, and as a way to reflect. Taro focuses on reflection.

## How the deck is organized

A tarot deck has 78 cards:

- **The Major Arcana**: 22 cards, from The Fool (0) to The World (21). They often stand for big themes and turning points, such as beginnings, balance, change and completion.
- **The Minor Arcana**: 56 cards in four suits of 14. Each suit has cards from Ace to Ten and four court cards: Page, Knight, Queen and King.
  - **Wands** (fire): energy, drive, creativity and ambition.
  - **Cups** (water): feelings, relationships and intuition.
  - **Swords** (air): thoughts, words, conflict and clarity.
  - **Pentacles** (earth): work, the body, resources and everyday life.

A card can appear **upright** or **reversed** (upside down). A reversed card often points to the same theme turned inward, blocked, delayed, or in need of a different approach. If you prefer to work only with upright cards, you can turn reversed cards off in Settings.

Taro's deck uses original art made for the app, and every card text was written for Taro.

## Using tarot for reflection

A tarot card doesn't know anything about you. What it can do is offer an image and a set of ideas that you hold up against your own situation. Often the most useful part of a reading is what you notice in yourself when you read it: what feels familiar, what you resist, what you had not thought about.

Some ways to get more from a reading:

- **Ask open questions.** "What can I learn from this situation?" gives you more to work with than "Will this work out?". Questions that start with "what" or "how" usually work well.
- **Stay with the question you care about.** Drawing again and again for the same question tends to blur things rather than clarify them.
- **Read the cards together.** In a spread, each position gives a card a role, such as "Past" or "Challenge". Notice how the cards relate to one another.
- **Treat "future" and "outcome" as a direction, not fate.** These positions describe where things may be heading if nothing changes. Your choices can change them.
- **Write it down.** Your journal keeps every reading and daily card with your notes. Over time, the Patterns view shows which cards and suits come up most in your draws. These are patterns in what you drew, not predictions.

## The daily card and Learn

Your daily card is free, needs no internet connection and uses no AI. It shows the card's name, keywords, a short meaning and a reflection question written for Taro.

Learn contains the full text for all 78 cards, upright and reversed, with notes on relationships, work and personal growth, plus a guide to each spread and its positions. Learn works completely offline.

## How AI readings work

When you ask for an AI reading, Taro sends four things to its server: your question (if you wrote one), the spread, the cards you drew with their orientation, and your app language. The server asks OpenAI's GPT models to write an interpretation of the whole spread. The AI is given Taro's own card names, keywords and short meanings and a description of each position, and it is instructed to write in a reflective voice, to refer to the cards you drew, and to avoid predictions and advice.

A few things to know about privacy:

- Taro never sends your name, email address or advertising ID with a reading.
- Your question is not stored on Taro's server.
- The finished reading is kept on the server, encrypted, only until your phone has received it (at most 7 days), and is then deleted.
- If you choose to report a reading, your question and that reading are kept for 90 days so they can be reviewed.
- OpenAI does not use this data to train its models.
- Your full history, questions and notes stay on your device.

AI readings need your permission. You can allow or turn off AI data sharing at any time in **Settings → Privacy & data → AI readings**. Without it, you can still use the daily card, Learn and your journal, and you can choose a **Classic reading**: the same draw, with the authored meaning of each card in its position, created on your phone without AI.

## What AI readings can't do

AI readings are generated text. They can be thoughtful and useful, but they have real limits:

- **They can be wrong or unexpected.** The AI can misread a situation, repeat itself, or say something that doesn't fit. Take what is useful and leave the rest.
- **They don't know you.** The AI only sees your question and the cards. It has no memory of your past readings and no knowledge of your life.
- **They can't see the future.** No reading can tell you what will occur, and Taro's readings never try to.
- **They don't answer some questions.** Taro doesn't give readings on health, pregnancy, death, legal matters, money decisions or gambling. When a question falls into one of these areas, the app explains why and suggests a way to rephrase it, and no reading is used. For those topics, please talk to a qualified professional.
- **They are not a substitute for support.** If you are going through something painful, talking with someone you trust can help. If you are thinking about harming yourself or someone else, please reach out now: **Settings → Help → Support lines** lists helplines for your region.

If a reading seems harmful or inappropriate, use **Report this reading** in the reading's menu. Reports help improve Taro.

## Disclaimer

Taro is for entertainment and self-reflection. It does not predict the future and is not a substitute for professional advice. Readings are not medical, legal, financial or psychological advice. Every decision you make remains yours.

# Frequently asked questions

## Readings and credits

### How do free readings work?

You get free AI readings every day. The balance at the top of Home shows how many free readings you have left today and how many purchased or earned readings you have. Free readings are used first. They reset at midnight in your time zone, and the app shows how long it is until the next one. The daily card is always free and never uses a reading.

### Does every spread cost the same?

Yes. Every AI reading uses one reading from your balance, from a single card up to the Celtic Cross. A reading is only used when your interpretation has arrived on your phone. If Taro can't create or deliver it, or declines your question, nothing is used.

### Why did Taro decline my question?

Taro is a tool for reflection, so it doesn't give readings on health, pregnancy, death, legal matters, money decisions or gambling, and it doesn't answer requests for a yes-or-no verdict about the future. When that happens, no reading is used and the app suggests a way to rephrase. Open questions such as "What can I learn from this situation?" usually work well. You can also reflect on the cards without a question.

## Purchases, deleting the app and new devices

### Can I restore my purchased readings?

Readings are consumable purchases. Store rules don't let them be restored the way a one-time purchase can, so they are tied to this installation of Taro. **Restore purchases** (in **Settings → Readings** and in the Store) brings back **Remove Banner Ads**, but it can't bring back readings.

Please keep this in mind before deleting the app: deleting Taro can make your remaining readings unavailable on that installation, and it always removes your journal from the device unless you have exported a backup.

### What happens if I reinstall Taro on iPhone?

On the same iPhone, Taro normally recognizes the installation after a reinstall, so your balance, including today's free reading, comes back. Your journal does not come back unless you import a backup. If you set up a new iPhone by transferring your data from the old one, both phones may share the same balance and the same daily free reading. On a new iPhone set up without a transfer, Taro starts as a new installation; see "How do I move my readings to a new device?" below.

### What happens if I reinstall Taro on Android?

On Android, uninstalling Taro or clearing its storage starts a new installation, so your purchased and earned readings are no longer visible there, and your journal is removed unless you import a backup. Free daily readings are counted per device, so a reinstall doesn't add an extra free reading that day. If you had purchased readings, follow the steps below to move them.

### How do I move my readings to a new device?

1. Install Taro on the new device and sign in to the same App Store or Google Play account you used for the purchases.
2. Open **Settings → Help → Move readings from another device**. Taro checks your past purchases with the store.
3. If readings from those purchases belong to your old installation, Taro shows a transfer code.
4. Email the transfer code together with your **Support ID** (see below) using **Settings → Help → Help & FAQ → Email support**.
5. Support moves your unused purchased readings to the new installation and replies when it's done.

An order number on its own isn't enough to move readings. Earned readings and free readings can't be moved.

### How do I restore Remove Banner Ads?

Open **Settings → Readings → Restore purchases** while signed in to the same store account. Banner ads disappear as soon as the purchase is found.

## Your journal and your data

### Where is my journal stored?

Only on your device. Taro has no accounts and no cloud sync, so your readings, daily cards, questions and notes are not kept on Taro's server. Exporting a backup is the way to keep a copy.

### How do I export and import my journal?

- **Export:** open **Settings → Privacy & data → Export backup**. Taro creates a file named like `taro-backup-2026-09-28.json` and opens the share sheet, so you can save it to Files, a cloud drive or email. No internet connection is needed.
- **Import:** open **Settings → Privacy & data → Import backup** and choose the file. Taro checks the file and shows a preview, such as how many readings and daily cards it contains. Then choose:
  - **Merge** adds the backup to what is already on this device. When the same entry exists in both, the newer version is kept.
  - **Replace** removes the journal on this device and uses the backup instead. Taro asks you to confirm first.

A backup contains your readings, daily cards, notes, favorites and settings. It does not contain your reading balance, purchases, privacy choices or Support ID, so importing a backup never changes your balance. Unfinished readings are not included. If a backup was made by a newer version of Taro, update the app before importing it.

### What does "Delete all data" do?

**Settings → Privacy & data → Delete all data** asks you to confirm twice. It then:

- erases your journal, notes, settings and scheduled reminders from this device;
- asks Taro's server to erase the reading history, rewarded-ad records and reports linked to this installation.

Your remaining readings and Remove Banner Ads are kept, because they are purchases. Today's free-reading count is also kept, so deleting data doesn't reset it. If you are offline, your device data is erased right away and the server request is sent when you are back online. To keep a copy of your journal, export a backup first.

## AI and privacy

### What does allowing AI readings share?

When you ask for an AI reading, Taro sends your question (if any), the spread, the cards you drew and your app language to its server, which asks OpenAI's GPT models to write the interpretation. Taro never sends your name, email address or advertising ID. Your question is not stored on Taro's server. The reading is kept encrypted only until your phone has received it (at most 7 days), then deleted. OpenAI does not use this data to train its models. The privacy policy in **Settings → Help → Legal** has the full details.

### Can I change my mind about AI consent?

Yes, at any time, in **Settings → Privacy & data → AI readings**. If you turn it off, nothing more is sent. The daily card, Learn and your journal keep working, and you can choose a **Classic reading**: the same draw with each card's authored meaning in its position, created on your phone without AI and without using a reading. If Taro updates what it shares, it asks for your consent again before the next AI reading.

### Are AI readings always right?

No. AI readings are generated text and can be wrong or unexpected. They are meant as prompts for your own reflection, not as answers or predictions. Take what is useful and leave the rest.

### How do I report a reading?

If an AI reading seems harmful, offensive or inappropriate, open the reading, tap the menu and choose **Report this reading**. Pick a reason, add a short note if you like (up to 500 characters) and tap Send. Your question and that reading are sent to Taro and kept for 90 days so they can be reviewed. You can send up to 10 reports a day, and each reading can be reported once. Classic readings can't be reported because they contain no AI text.

## Help and support

### What is my Support ID?

Your Support ID is a short 8-character code that identifies this installation of Taro without revealing anything about you. You can find it in **Settings → About**. It is added automatically when you use **Settings → Help → Help & FAQ → Email support**, together with the app version, your device's system version and your app language. Support asks for it when you need help with purchases or moving readings. It is not included in backups.

### How do I contact support?

Use **Settings → Help → Help & FAQ → Email support**. It opens an email with your Support ID and app details already filled in, so we can help you faster. Please don't include sensitive personal details in your message.

### Where can I find help if I'm struggling?

If you are thinking about harming yourself or someone else, please reach out now. **Settings → Help → Support lines** lists helplines for your region and an international directory. It works without an internet connection. If you are in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number.

### Is Taro professional advice?

No. Taro is for entertainment and self-reflection. It does not predict the future and is not a substitute for professional advice. Readings are not medical, legal, financial or psychological advice.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Fool can ask whether a fear of looking silly has started to shrink your world. It may also reflect restlessness that jumps from one new thing to the next without letting any of them take root. You might notice which pattern feels familiar, and experiment with its gentle opposite for a week.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card celebrates the beginner's mind. It may invite you to try something where you have no reputation to protect: a new skill, a different route home, a question asked out loud. Growth here comes from staying curious and letting yourself be surprised, rather than from getting everything right on the first try.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to hesitation about letting someone in, or to moving so quickly that the other person has little room to keep pace. You might notice whether you are protecting yourself by staying vague, or skipping over the slower parts of getting to know someone. A gentle check-in about pace, yours and theirs, could open space for both of you.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Fool can reflect a playful, unguarded quality: meeting someone without a script, or letting a familiar bond surprise you again. It may invite you to bring curiosity to the people close to you, asking questions you assume you already know the answers to. Openness here is not naivety; it is a willingness to be present without deciding in advance how things should go.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Fool may reflect an idea that keeps being postponed until conditions feel perfect, or a leap made without checking the basics. You might consider whether you need more information or simply more courage. Writing down the smallest possible first step, and one practical safeguard, can turn a vague wish into something you can test without betting everything on it.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in any project, the Fool can reflect the start of something unfamiliar: a new role, a course, a creative idea with no track record yet. It invites you to treat early mistakes as information rather than verdicts. You might ask what you would try if the first attempt were allowed to be rough, and who could help you learn the ropes along the way.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Fool is imagined at the edge of a high place with open sky ahead, mid-stride, carrying only a small bundle. A small companion animal at their heels can stand for instinct, playful or cautionary. A single white flower may suggest innocence and openness, while the wide horizon and morning light speak of possibility. The figure's upturned face invites the viewer to ask what they are looking toward, and what they have chosen not to carry.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Fool may show the spark of a new beginning that has not quite caught. You might feel pulled toward something fresh while also standing very still, turning the idea over and waiting for a sign that it is safe to move. Sometimes that waiting is wise; sometimes it has quietly become a habit.
This position can also reflect the opposite tilt: energy that rushes ahead without looking, saying yes to everything and leaving little room to notice where your feet land. Both tilts share a question about readiness and trust.
You may want to ask which of these feels closer right now. If you are holding back, what is one small, low-stakes way to test the water? If you are racing, what would it look like to keep your enthusiasm and add one moment of pause before the next leap?
cards.meaningUpright:
The Fool stands at the very beginning of the Major Arcana, numbered zero, before any lesson has been learned. It is the energy of someone setting out with a light bag and an open face, more interested in what the road might show than in knowing exactly where it ends.
In everyday life this card can reflect the first week in a new place, a hobby picked up with no plan to master it, or a conversation you start without rehearsing every line. It may point to a part of you that is ready to try, even while another part asks for a certainty that no one can offer. Here, not knowing is not a flaw; it is simply where every journey starts.
This card invites you to consider where a little more lightness could help. What would change if you allowed yourself to be a beginner again, to ask basic questions and to learn by doing? The Fool does not ask you to ignore common sense. It asks you to notice whether fear of getting it wrong is keeping you from taking any step at all.
cards.name: The Fool
reflectionQuestions: What would you try if you were allowed to be a beginner?
Who in your life makes it easier to take a small risk, and why?
What is one low-stakes first step you could take this week?
cards.shortReversed: A pause at the edge: is it caution, or a fear of looking foolish?
cards.shortUpright: A step into something new, taken with more curiosity than certainty.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Magician can reflect a gap between the person you know you could be and the habits you are living. It may ask where self-doubt is making you wait for permission. You might choose one skill to practice openly, imperfectly, and notice how confidence grows from doing rather than from waiting to feel ready.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card invites you to recognize your own agency. You might list the skills, habits and supports you already have, and notice how they could serve something you care about. Practice, repetition and clear intention are the Magician's quiet tools; small daily choices can add up to real change over time.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may ask whether words and actions are lining up in a close bond, yours or the other person's. It can also reflect holding back what you really think, or performing a version of yourself you believe will be liked. You might consider what would change if you let someone see your real intentions, even the uncertain ones.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Magician can reflect the power of clear, direct communication. It may invite you to say what you mean and to act in ways that match your words. You might notice how much you can shape the tone of a connection through small, deliberate gestures: a thoughtful message, a plan followed through, attention given without distraction.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Magician may reflect talent that is underused, or effort spread so thin that nothing quite lands. It can also point to a temptation to oversell or cut corners. You might ask which task truly deserves your energy right now, and what honest, steady work on it would look like over the next few days.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the Magician points to skill meeting opportunity. It may invite you to take stock of your abilities, contacts and resources, and to direct them toward one clear aim. This is a card of starting, pitching, building a prototype or finally writing the proposal. Focus and follow-through matter more here than having every answer in advance.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Magician is imagined at a crossroads market stall at dawn, arranging four humble objects for the four suits: a green branch, a clay cup, a knife for cutting bread and a single coin. One hand reaches toward the stall, the other gestures at the brightening sky, linking idea and action. Threads of light running between the objects suggest attention joining separate tools into one purpose, and an unfinished loaf hints that the making has only just begun.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Magician may reflect ability that is present but not yet in use. You might have the skills and the ideas, yet feel your energy leaking into too many directions, or doubt that your contribution counts. The table is set; the hands are not quite moving.
This card can also point to cleverness turned slightly sideways: using charm or quick talk to skip the part of the work that feels dull, or presenting a confident surface while feeling unsure inside. Neither is a moral failing. Both can be signs that intention and action have drifted apart.
You may want to look at where your focus is splitting. Choosing one small, concrete task and finishing it can rebuild trust in your own hands. It may also help to ask what you would do differently if no one were watching.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Magician is the card of turning an idea into something real. Where the Fool steps out with nothing planned, the Magician stops, looks at what is within reach and decides to use it. The traditional image of one hand raised and one pointing down suggests a bridge between intention and action, between what you imagine and what you can actually do today.
In daily life this card can reflect the moment a plan finally gets a date, a budget of time, a first draft. It may point to skills you tend to overlook because they come easily to you: a talent for explaining things, for fixing small problems, for bringing people together. Resourcefulness here means noticing that the pieces are already on the table.
This card invites you to consider where your attention goes. Focus is a kind of craft; it can be practiced. You might ask what one thing you would like to bring into being, and which of the tools you already have could move it one step closer. The Magician does not promise results. It highlights the power of showing up with intention and using what you have.
cards.name: The Magician
reflectionQuestions: Which of your skills do you tend to take for granted?
Where do your words and your actions not quite match right now?
What one intention could you act on today with what you already have?
cards.shortReversed: Your tools are on the table, but your attention may be elsewhere. What would help you gather it?
cards.shortUpright: You may already hold more of what you need than you think; this card asks what you want to make with it.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the High Priestess may ask whether you have been living mostly on the surface lately, reacting rather than reflecting. It can be a nudge to turn inward again, without pressure to find instant answers. You might set aside one quiet ritual this week and notice what shifts when you give yourself room to listen.
aspects.growthUpright: Growth with the High Priestess tends to begin in stillness. You might experiment with a few minutes each day of simply noticing your thoughts, breath or surroundings without trying to fix anything. Over time, this kind of attention can help you tell the difference between anxious chatter and a steadier inner sense.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to things left unsaid between you and someone close, or to a habit of reading between the lines instead of asking directly. You might consider whether a gentle, honest question could replace guesswork. It can also reflect a need to protect your inner world while still letting someone see a little more of it.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the High Priestess can reflect a bond where much is understood without words, or a moment when listening matters more than speaking. It may invite you to notice the undercurrents: what a friend's silence might mean, or what your own reluctance is protecting. You might offer someone close the gift of unhurried attention.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the High Priestess can reflect second-guessing a sound instinct because others are louder, or information being kept back in a team. You might ask what you know about a situation that you have not voiced. Finding a calm, appropriate way to share it could make the work clearer for everyone, including you.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the High Priestess may suggest that not every decision needs to be made today. It can invite you to observe, gather impressions and trust your sense of timing. Reflective work such as research, writing, planning or mentoring fits this card well. Quiet competence and discretion may be valued more than you realize.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's High Priestess is imagined seated at the threshold of a moonlit doorway, half in light and half in shadow, with a closed book resting on the knees. Behind the figure, a curtain stirs as if something waits beyond it. A crescent moon reflected in a still basin can echo cycles and intuition, and deep blue tones suggest calm on the surface with depth below. The figure's quiet, attentive stillness is the center of the image.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the High Priestess may suggest that your inner voice is present but hard to hear. Busy days, other people's opinions or a steady stream of screens can crowd out the stillness this card needs. You might notice that you keep asking others what to do about something you partly know already.
This card can also point to holding something in for too long: a feeling, a question or a truth that has stayed hidden and now feels heavy. Privacy is healthy; secrecy that isolates you may deserve a second look.
You may want to create a small pocket of quiet and see what surfaces. It can help to write without editing, or to ask yourself one simple question and wait for the first honest answer. What have you sensed that you have not yet let yourself say?
cards.meaningUpright:
The High Priestess sits between two pillars, at the threshold of what is known and what is still hidden. This figure does not act or explain; its gift is attention: the kind of deep, patient listening that notices what lies beneath the surface of a situation, a conversation or a feeling.
In everyday life, this card may reflect a hunch you cannot fully justify, a sense that something is not being said, or a dream that lingers into the afternoon. It can point to moments when the answer is not found by gathering more information, but by sitting quietly with what you already have. Some things become clear only when you stop pushing for clarity.
This card invites you to trust the slower, less verbal parts of yourself. You might make time for journaling, a walk without headphones, or simply a pause before replying. Inner knowing is not a replacement for facts, and it can sit alongside them. The High Priestess asks you to notice what your quieter voice has been trying to tell you, and to give it a little room before you decide what to do.
cards.name: The High Priestess
reflectionQuestions: What do you sense about your situation that you have not said out loud?
Whose silence, including your own, might be worth listening to more closely?
Where could you make ten quiet minutes for yourself this week?
cards.shortReversed: Outside noise may be drowning out a quieter voice inside you; a little silence could help.
cards.shortUpright: A quiet invitation to listen to what you already sense but have not yet put into words.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Empress may be a gentle reminder that you deserve the same patience you give to others. It can reflect feeling out of touch with your own needs or doubting your creative worth. You might start with one small, kind ritual that belongs only to you, and see how it changes your week.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Empress invites you to enjoy being in your body and in the physical world. Rest, good food, time in nature and simple pleasures are not indulgences here; they are ways of recharging. You might notice what helps you feel grounded and generous, and make a little more room for it.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, the Empress may ask whether care in a relationship has become one-sided, or whether concern has slipped into managing someone else's choices. You might consider where you could step back and trust the other person more, and where you could ask more openly for the care you need yourself.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Empress can reflect warmth, affection and a sense of being cared for, or of caring for others with generosity. It may invite you to create comfort together: shared meals, time outdoors, small gestures of tenderness. You might notice how the people close to you like to be looked after, and how you like to be looked after too.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, this card may reflect burnout from looking after everyone's projects but your own, or a creative block that no amount of pushing seems to shift. You might ask what would make the work feel nourishing again: a change of setting, a shorter to-do list, or permission to make something imperfect.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a creative project, the Empress points to fertile ground. It may reflect a time when ideas grow easily, when you can nurture a team, a garden of projects or a slow, rewarding piece of craft. It invites you to make your working space more comfortable and to value the kind of progress that comes from steady, patient attention.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Empress is imagined as a figure at rest in a kitchen garden in late summer, surrounded by ripening vegetables, a loaf cooling on a sill and a stream running past. Soft woven fabrics and a basket of just-picked fruit suggest comfort and the pleasure of the senses, while bees moving between flowers hint at growth that happens through many small acts of care. The mood is warm and unhurried, inviting the viewer to notice abundance already present.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Empress may reflect care that has lost its balance. You might be pouring energy into everyone and everything except yourself, until creativity feels dry and even pleasant things seem like chores. Or care might tip into over-involvement, holding on so tightly that there is little space for others to grow in their own way.
This card can also point to a creative project that has stalled, or to a disconnection from the simple, physical comforts that usually steady you.
You may want to look at where your care is going and whether any of it could come home. A small act of tending to yourself, such as a nourishing meal, a slow walk, or a few minutes of making something just for fun, can be a way to reconnect with the Empress's generous energy.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Empress is the card of growth that happens through care. Where the High Priestess listens inward, the Empress turns outward to the living world: gardens, meals, handmade things, the pleasure of good bread or warm sunlight. This card stands for the kind of creativity that nourishes, whether it is a project, a home, a friendship or your own sense of ease.
In daily life this card may reflect a season of making: cooking for friends, sketching again, looking after plants or people, or simply noticing that you feel more at home in your body than usual. It can also point to patience. The Empress knows that growth takes its own time, and that pulling at a seedling does not make it grow faster.
This card invites you to consider what you are cultivating and how you are cultivating it. You might ask where a little more softness, beauty or rest could help something flourish. Abundance here is less about having a lot and more about noticing and enjoying what is already alive around you.
cards.name: The Empress
reflectionQuestions: What is growing in your life right now that deserves some patience?
How do you like to be cared for, and have you told anyone?
What simple pleasure could you make time for today?
cards.shortReversed: Care may be flowing outward while your own well is running low. Where could some of it return to you?
cards.shortUpright: Something is growing, in you or around you. This card invites you to tend it with patience and warmth.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Emperor may ask whether you are being too strict with yourself, or not strict enough. Self-discipline that turns harsh can drain energy, while having no structure can leave you feeling unmoored. You might look for the middle path: a framework firm enough to hold you and gentle enough to live with.
aspects.growthUpright: One quiet form of growth is becoming a steady presence for yourself. Routines, self-discipline and keeping promises to yourself can build a quiet kind of confidence. You might choose one habit that supports the life you want and give it a simple, reliable structure.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may ask whether one person in a relationship is setting most of the terms. You might notice patterns of control, stubbornness or silent rule-making, on either side. A calm conversation about what each of you needs to feel respected could help rebalance things without turning it into a contest.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Emperor can reflect reliability: being someone others can count on, and valuing people who show up consistently for you. It may invite you to talk about shared agreements, such as how you divide tasks, handle plans or respect each other's time. Clear boundaries can make closeness feel safer, not colder.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Emperor may reflect a workplace that feels overly rigid, or your own tendency to micromanage when stressed. It can also point to frustration with authority. You might ask which rules actually serve the work, and where you could offer or request more flexibility in a constructive way.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the Emperor points to organization and ownership. It may be a good moment to set priorities, define roles or build a system that makes daily work easier. Leadership here looks like steadiness, fairness and following through on your word, whether or not you hold a formal title.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Emperor is imagined as a figure seated at a sturdy stone table set into a hillside, with a map, a measuring rod and a lamp laid out in careful order. Dry-stone walls running across the fields behind show boundaries built by hand, stone by stone. A ram grazing nearby can nod to Aries and the drive to begin. Warm reds suggest vitality, and a small gate left open in one wall hints that firm structures can still let people through.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Emperor may reflect structure that has become too heavy. Plans can harden into rigid rules, and a need for safety can turn into a need to control every detail, your own or other people's. You might notice irritation when things do not go exactly as arranged.
This card can also point to the opposite: a lack of structure where some would help, or feeling that others make the rules while you follow. Either way, the question is about healthy authority and where it sits.
You may want to look at one area where the balance feels off. If it is too tight, what could you loosen without losing what matters? If it is too loose, what small routine or boundary would give you firmer ground? Reclaiming authority can begin with a single, clear decision.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Emperor sits on a solid seat and looks straight ahead. Where the Empress lets things grow, this card gives them a frame to grow within: routines, agreements, a roof and walls. It is the energy of taking responsibility, of deciding what the rules of your own life are and keeping to them.
In everyday life this card may reflect setting up a budget of time, writing a plan for a project, or being the steady person others lean on in a busy week. It can point to moments when saying a firm, calm "no" protects something you value. Structure here is not about control for its own sake; it is about creating enough stability that you and the people around you can breathe.
This card invites you to consider where a bit more order would help. You might ask which boundaries need clarifying, which commitments you truly want to keep, and how you can lead with fairness rather than force. The Emperor also reminds you that authority over your own life is something you can claim, step by step, without waiting for someone else to hand it to you.
cards.name: The Emperor
reflectionQuestions: Which boundary in your life would benefit from being stated more clearly?
Where do you feel you have authority, and where do you give it away?
What one routine could give your week a steadier shape?
cards.shortReversed: Rules that once helped may now feel tight. What would a kinder, sturdier structure look like?
cards.shortUpright: A time to build some structure around what matters, and to take calm ownership of your choices.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Hierophant may be a nudge to write your own guidelines. It can reflect a moment of outgrowing a belief or an old role. You might list the values you truly hold today, in your own words, and notice where they overlap with what you were taught and where they gently part ways.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card invites you to learn from those who came before you. Books, teachers, communities and practices can offer frameworks that support your development. You might choose one discipline or tradition to study with patience, noticing what it offers before deciding what to make of it.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to tension between what is expected of a relationship and what actually feels true for the people in it. You might consider whether you are following outside norms that do not fit your situation. An honest conversation about the kind of bond you both want can make room for your own way of doing things.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Hierophant can reflect shared values, commitments and the rituals that hold people together: family traditions, anniversaries, weekly calls. It may invite you to notice what you and someone close both believe in, and how you honor it. Guidance from a trusted friend or elder could also be helpful now.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Hierophant may reflect frustration with how things have always been done, or a sense that the official path does not suit you. You might ask which rules protect quality and which simply resist change. Proposing a better approach, calmly and with evidence, can be more effective than working around the system.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in study, the Hierophant highlights learning a craft properly, respecting established methods and finding a mentor. It may be a good time to take a course, earn a qualification or ask someone experienced to show you the ropes. Being part of a team or institution can offer support as well as structure.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Hierophant is imagined as a teacher in a quiet courtyard, sitting on a worn stone bench beneath an old tree, with a small circle of listeners of different ages. A heavy key hangs from the teacher's belt, a symbol of understanding passed on through study and practice. Books stacked on the bench and a bell in the arch above suggest shared ritual and learning. An open gate at the far side of the courtyard hints that every teaching can lead somewhere new.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Hierophant may reflect a growing distance from the rules or expectations you grew up with. Something that once felt right may now seem too narrow, or you might sense that you have been following a script more out of habit than conviction.
This card can also point to the opposite tilt: rejecting every convention so firmly that you miss what could still be useful in it. Questioning is healthy; it tends to work well when it is curious rather than reactive.
You may want to look at one expectation that feels heavy and ask where it came from. Does it still reflect your values, or someone else's? Finding your own way can include keeping the parts that still serve you and letting go, with respect, of the parts that no longer do.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Hierophant is the card of shared knowledge: the ways of doing things that a community passes from one generation to the next. It can stand for teachers, mentors, institutions, rituals and codes of practice, anything that helps people learn together and feel they belong to something larger than themselves.
In everyday life this card may reflect joining a class, following a recipe handed down in a family, asking an experienced colleague for guidance or marking a milestone with a familiar ceremony. It can point to the comfort of not having to invent everything alone. Traditions carry the lessons of many people, and there is often good sense in them.
This card invites you to consider what you have inherited and what you have chosen. You might ask which shared values give your life steadiness, and whom you could learn from right now. The Hierophant is not about blind obedience; it highlights the value of learning a form well, whether you keep it, adapt it or eventually pass it on in your own words.
cards.name: The Hierophant
reflectionQuestions: Which values did you inherit, and which have you chosen for yourself?
Who has taught you something important, and what did you learn from how they taught it?
What is one expectation you would like to examine more closely this week?
cards.shortReversed: An inherited rule may no longer fit. This card invites you to test it against what you truly value.
cards.shortUpright: There may be wisdom in what others have walked before you. What tradition or teacher could help right now?

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Lovers can reflect inner conflict: part of you wanting change, part wanting comfort. Neither part is wrong. You might give each a voice, on paper or in conversation, and see if there is a choice that honors both, even if only partly.
aspects.growthUpright: Knowing your own values more clearly is the inner work this card points toward. When you understand what matters to you, choices become less about pleasing others and more about staying true to yourself. You might write down three values and notice where they already guide your days.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to a gap between two people's hopes or priorities, or to feelings that have not been voiced. You might consider whether you are adapting too much to keep the peace, or expecting someone to guess what you need. An open, kind conversation about values could help you both see where you stand.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Lovers can reflect deep mutual understanding and the pleasure of choosing each other, whether in romance, friendship or family. It may invite you to share what you truly value and to listen to what the other person values too. Closeness grows when both people can be honest and still feel welcome.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Lovers may reflect friction in a partnership or a sense that your work does not match what you care about. It can also point to hesitation over a choice between two paths. You might list what each path would ask of you, and notice which one you feel more willing to give that to.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the Lovers highlights collaboration and choices rooted in your values. It may reflect a partnership that brings out the good in both people, or a decision about which direction to follow. You might ask which option feels meaningful as well as practical, and let both count in your choice.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Lovers is imagined as two figures standing on either side of a narrow stream, reaching to clasp hands across it, drawn so that anyone can see themselves in either figure. Above them, two birds circle in the same bright sky. On one bank grows a fruit tree and on the other a flowering vine, two different gifts meeting in the middle. The stream suggests the choice and the effort that real connection asks of both people.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Lovers may reflect a sense of being pulled in two directions. What you want and what you think you should want might not match, or a close bond may feel slightly out of tune, with each person valuing different things without saying so.
This card can also point to a decision that keeps being postponed, perhaps because choosing one option means letting go of another. Avoiding the choice can feel easier in the short term while quietly draining energy.
You may want to write down what each option honestly offers and asks of you, and which of your values it supports. It can help to notice where you feel most like yourself. Realignment often begins with a small, truthful admission, first to yourself and then, if it feels right, to someone else.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Lovers is often read as a card of romance, but its deeper theme is alignment: the meeting of two parts, two people or two paths in a way that feels whole. It asks what you value most, and whether the choices in front of you reflect it. Connection here is both with others and with yourself.
In everyday life this card may reflect a relationship where you feel truly seen, a partnership at work where ideas flow easily, or a decision that requires you to say clearly what matters to you. It can point to a moment of choosing between two good options, where there is no obvious right answer, only the one that fits who you are becoming.
This card invites you to consider how honest you are being with yourself and others. You might ask what you are drawn toward and why, and what you are willing to commit to. The Lovers highlights that meaningful choices are rarely about perfection. They are about bringing your heart and your judgment into the same room and letting them talk.
cards.name: The Lovers
reflectionQuestions: Which of your values feels most important to honor right now?
Where in a close relationship could you be a little more honest about what you want?
What choice have you been postponing, and what would help you make it?
cards.shortReversed: Part of you may want one thing and part another. This card invites you to listen to both before choosing.
cards.shortUpright: A choice made from the heart and the head together, in line with what you truly value.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Chariot may ask whether you are driving yourself too hard or letting others set your course. It can be an invitation to reconnect with your own reasons for going where you are going. You might check in with yourself each morning and ask which direction feels truly yours today.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card invites you to practice self-direction. Knowing what you want and holding your different moods and motives together is a skill. You might choose one meaningful goal and notice how you keep yourself on course, celebrating each small stretch of road you cover.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to two people pulling in different directions, or to one person steering while the other feels carried along. You might consider whether you are pushing a relationship toward a goal before both of you are ready. Slowing down to agree on the destination could ease the strain.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Chariot can reflect a shared sense of direction: moving through a busy or challenging period together, each supporting the other's goals. It may invite you to talk about where you are both heading and how to keep pace with each other. Commitment here looks like steady effort and mutual encouragement.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Chariot may reflect a project losing momentum or a sense of rushing without a clear plan. It can also point to conflicting priorities from different people. You might step back, clarify what success actually looks like, and decide which tasks move you toward it and which only keep you busy.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the Chariot highlights drive and focused effort. It may reflect a phase of pushing a project over the line, competing in a healthy way or keeping a team moving together. You might set a clear aim, gather your resources and give yourself a realistic timeline of your own choosing.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Chariot is imagined as a figure driving a small, sturdy cart along a coastal road, drawn by two animals of contrasting temperament, one calm and one restless. The driver holds the reins lightly, steering with attention rather than force. A shell-like canopy over the seat may nod to Cancer and the protection that lets someone move forward safely, while the open road and distant harbor lights suggest a destination chosen, not imposed.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Chariot may reflect momentum that has stalled or scattered. You might feel busy but not quite moving, pulled between too many goals, or unsure which direction is really yours. The reins are there, but they may feel loose.
This card can also point to pushing too hard: forcing progress through sheer effort while ignoring signs that the route needs adjusting. Willpower alone can take you a long way, yet it tires when it is not paired with clarity.
You may want to pause and name the forces pulling at you. Which ones matter most right now, and which could wait? Choosing one clear direction for the coming days, and allowing yourself to set the others down for a while, can help you feel steady in the driver's seat again.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Chariot is the card of moving forward with purpose. Its traditional image shows two animals pulling a vehicle, often in different colors, as if each wanted to go its own way. The driver's task is not to fight them but to guide them together. That is the heart of this card: turning inner tension into steady direction.
In everyday life this card may reflect a week when you finally commit to a goal and keep at it despite distractions: training for an event, finishing a big assignment, moving house or making a change you have talked about for a long time. It can point to the discipline of balancing competing needs, such as ambition and rest, or excitement and caution, rather than letting one win completely.
This card invites you to consider where you want to go and what is pulling you off course. You might ask how you can use your mixed feelings as fuel rather than as brakes. The Chariot highlights focus and will, and also the quiet protection of knowing yourself well enough to steer.
cards.name: The Chariot
reflectionQuestions: Which two parts of you are pulling in different directions right now?
Who is traveling alongside you, and how are you supporting each other?
What single direction could you commit to for the next few days?
cards.shortReversed: Energy may be pulling in several directions at once. Where could you gently take back the reins?
cards.shortUpright: Momentum is possible when you hold your different drives together and point them in one direction.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, Strength may be a reminder that confidence can dip and return. It can reflect a stretch of self-doubt or harsh inner criticism. You might keep a short list of moments when you coped well, and read it on difficult days, as evidence of the steadiness you already have.
aspects.growthUpright: Strength suggests befriending your own inner lion rather than caging it: the strong feelings, desires and instincts that make you who you are. Rather than fighting them, you might get curious about what they need. Self-compassion is not weakness here; it is a practice that makes courage more sustainable.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to short tempers, or to someone swallowing their feelings to avoid conflict. You might consider whether you are being too hard on yourself or on someone close. Speaking up kindly, before frustration builds, can protect the connection and your own sense of steadiness.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, Strength can reflect patience and warmth that help people feel safe with you. It may invite you to meet someone's difficult moods with calm rather than matching their intensity, while still holding your own boundaries. Gentle firmness can build trust over time.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, Strength may reflect feeling worn down by pressure, or doubting your ability to cope with a challenge. It can also point to reacting sharply under stress. You might ask what support or rest would help you recover your footing, and how to set a pace you can keep.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, Strength highlights persistence and emotional maturity. It may reflect handling a demanding task or person with patience and grace, or leading by encouragement rather than pressure. You might trust that steady, consistent effort counts, even when no one is watching.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Strength is imagined as a calm figure kneeling in a sunlit meadow beside a large lion, one hand resting on its mane while the animal leans in, relaxed and trusting. No ropes or chains appear; the bond is shown through closeness and ease. Wildflowers growing around both of them suggest that patience lets gentler things flourish. Warm golden light keeps the mood peaceful, showing power and gentleness side by side.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, Strength may reflect a time when your usual steadiness feels harder to find. Patience might run out quickly, or you might hear an inner voice that is sharper and more critical than usual. The lion is restless, and so are you.
This card can also point to courage turned inward and not yet expressed: you may be stronger than you feel, but doubting yourself has made it hard to show. Or it can reflect an effort to hold everything together through willpower alone, which tends to wear thin.
You may want to notice how you speak to yourself when things are hard. What would change if you used the tone you would use with a frightened friend? Rebuilding courage often starts with small acts of self-kindness, and with asking for support when the load is heavy.
cards.meaningUpright:
Strength is a card of courage, but not the loud kind. Its traditional image shows a figure calmly resting a hand on a lion, not overpowering it but soothing it. The strength here comes from patience, warmth and a steady presence that can meet wild energy, whether someone else's or your own, without panic.
In everyday life this card may reflect staying calm in a tense conversation, keeping a promise when it has become inconvenient, or sitting with a strong feeling long enough to understand it rather than act on it straight away. It can point to the quiet confidence of someone who does not need to prove anything. Taming the lion is less about suppressing it and more about befriending it.
This card invites you to consider how you respond to pressure. You might ask where compassion, including compassion for yourself, could be more effective than force. Strength suggests that softness and firmness can live together, and that the most lasting kind of courage is often steady, kind and persistent.
cards.name: Strength
reflectionQuestions: What would gentle courage look like in the situation on your mind?
Whose difficult mood are you meeting, and how could you stay steady with them?
What kind words could you offer yourself today?
cards.shortReversed: Your inner steadiness may feel thin right now. Gentleness toward yourself could be a strong place to start.
cards.shortUpright: Courage does not always roar. Sometimes it looks like patience, kindness and staying with something hard.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Hermit may ask whether you are hiding from yourself or from others. It can reflect a need to balance reflection with connection. You might plan one quiet ritual and one small social moment this week, and notice how each one feels. Balance here is personal; only you can sense the right mix.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card invites a practice of solitude and self-inquiry. Journaling, walking, or simply sitting quietly with a question can help you understand yourself better. You might think of your own lantern as a single insight you have gained recently, and let it light your next step.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to withdrawal that others feel as distance, or to loneliness you have not mentioned. You might consider whether you have been waiting for someone else to reach out. A short, honest message can reopen a door, even if you still need some quiet time afterward.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Hermit can reflect a need for space to think, and the value of people who respect that need. It may invite you to explain gently that stepping back is about reflection, not rejection. Time alone can help you return to others with more clarity about what you want and can offer.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Hermit may reflect working in isolation for too long, or missing input that could help. It can also point to overthinking a decision. You might ask a trusted colleague or mentor for a fresh view, and notice how sharing your ideas can sharpen them.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in study, the Hermit highlights deep, focused work and independent thinking. It may be a good moment for research, writing, planning or learning something thoroughly. You might protect some uninterrupted time and notice what insights come when you are not constantly responding to others.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Hermit is imagined as a cloaked figure on a high, snowy ridge at dusk, holding a simple lantern that lights only the next few steps of the path. A walking stick worn smooth by use suggests support gathered from experience. Footprints in the snow behind show how far the figure has already come. Cool blues and grays speak of solitude and clear air, while the lantern's warm glow shows that insight can be carried into even the darkest stretch of the road.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Hermit may reflect solitude that has lasted longer than it helps. Time alone can slowly shift into withdrawal, where reaching out feels harder each day. You might notice that you are thinking in circles rather than toward something.
This card can also point to the opposite: keeping so busy or so surrounded by others that there is no room for reflection at all. Avoiding quiet can be a way of avoiding a question you are not ready to face.
You may want to look at which side feels closer. If you have been alone a lot, what is one small, comfortable way to reconnect with someone? If you have been avoiding stillness, what could you learn from ten minutes alone with your thoughts? The lantern is still yours to lift.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Hermit walks alone on a mountain path, holding a lantern that lights just the next few steps. This card is about stepping back from the noise to look for your own answers. The Hermit is not lonely so much as purposeful: the withdrawal has a reason, and the light is carried, not waited for.
In everyday life this card may reflect choosing a quiet evening over a busy one, taking a solo walk to think through a decision, or spending time with a book, a notebook or a craft that asks for concentration. It can point to a season of reassessing priorities, when other people's opinions matter less than your own slowly forming sense of what is true for you.
This card invites you to consider what you are searching for and whether you have given yourself enough space to find it. You might ask what one question you would bring on a long walk. The Hermit suggests that wisdom often arrives in small, steady glimpses, like a lantern showing the path one step at a time, and that this is enough to keep going.
cards.name: The Hermit
reflectionQuestions: What question would you take with you on a long, quiet walk?
Who respects your need for space, and how could you let them know you value it?
Where could you protect one uninterrupted hour for yourself this week?
cards.shortReversed: Solitude may have tipped into isolation, or into avoiding the quiet altogether. What balance feels right?
cards.shortUpright: A little time apart could help you hear your own thoughts more clearly.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Wheel may ask whether you are trying to control what cannot be controlled. It can reflect a wish for certainty during a changing time. You might practice letting go of one thing you cannot influence, and putting that energy into one thing you can.
aspects.growthUpright: Seeing your life as a series of cycles, rather than one straight line, can be freeing. Noticing your own rhythms, such as when you feel energized or when you need rest, can help you plan with them rather than against them. You might map the last year and notice its turning points.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to familiar conflicts that keep returning, or to resistance to a relationship changing shape. You might consider what pattern you and someone close tend to repeat, and what each of you could try differently. Change does not have to mean loss; it can mean growth.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Wheel can reflect a new phase: getting closer, moving to a different stage or simply adjusting to changing circumstances. It may invite you to stay flexible and to talk openly about how things are shifting. Relationships, like seasons, have rhythms, and naming them can help you move through them together.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Wheel may reflect frustration with delays or a feeling that effort is not paying off. It can also point to repeating the same approach and expecting a different result. You might review what has worked before, what has not, and where a small change in method could shift the pattern.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the Wheel highlights shifting circumstances and new openings. It may reflect a change in plans, a new team or a project that suddenly moves forward. You might stay alert to opportunities while remembering that every phase, busy or slow, has something to offer.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Wheel of Fortune is imagined as a great turning wheel set in a sky that shifts from dawn at one edge to night at the other, showing every phase at once. Small figures and creatures ride its rim, some rising and some descending, none staying still. Symbols of the four seasons in the corners may frame the idea of natural cycles. At the hub, a calm, unmoving center suggests the steady perspective that can be found even while everything turns.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Wheel of Fortune may reflect a sense of being stuck in a loop or resisting a change that is already under way. You might feel that events are happening to you, or notice that the same frustrating pattern keeps returning in different clothes.
This card can also point to holding on tightly to a good phase, fearing that it cannot last. Clinging makes the natural turning feel harder.
You may want to look at what is within your reach. Patterns often repeat until something in how we respond shifts, even slightly. It can help to name the cycle you see, notice your part in it without blame, and choose one small thing to do differently. You cannot stop the wheel, but you can find firmer footing on it.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Wheel of Fortune is the card of cycles. Seasons turn, moods rise and fall, busy periods give way to quiet ones. Nothing stays at the top or the bottom for ever. This card reminds you that change is a normal part of life, and that some of it is outside anyone's control while some of it responds to how you meet it.
In everyday life this card may reflect a turning point: a chapter closing and another opening, a lucky break that shifts your plans, or an unexpected setback that changes your pace. It can also point to recognizing a pattern that has shown up before, such as the same kind of situation arriving in a new form, and seeing it with fresh eyes.
This card invites you to consider where you are on your own wheel right now. You might ask what this phase is asking of you, and what it could be teaching you. The Wheel does not decide your life for you. It highlights that flexibility, perspective and a sense of humor can help you ride the turns, and that a hard season is a season, not a permanent state.
cards.name: Wheel of Fortune
reflectionQuestions: What cycle or season do you feel you are in right now?
Which pattern keeps returning in your relationships, and what might it ask of you?
What is one thing within your control that you could focus on this week?
cards.shortReversed: A familiar pattern may be coming round again. What could you do differently this time?
cards.shortUpright: Things are turning. This card invites you to notice the cycle you are in and how you want to move with it.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, Justice may ask whether you hold yourself to a much stricter standard than you hold others. It can reflect guilt that lingers after a lesson has already been learned. You might practice fair self-assessment: naming both what went wrong and what went right.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card invites you to live by your values and take ownership of your choices. Reflecting on the effects of your actions, without harshness, can help you grow. You might look at one recent decision and ask what you would keep, and what you might do differently next time.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to an imbalance, such as one person doing more of the emotional or practical work, or a conflict where blame feels one-sided. You might consider what fairness would look like from both points of view, and whether an apology or a clearer agreement could restore balance.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, Justice can reflect balance and mutual respect: both people giving and receiving in a way that feels fair. It may invite you to look honestly at how responsibilities and care are shared. Clear, kind conversations about expectations can strengthen trust and prevent quiet resentment.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, Justice may reflect frustration with unfair treatment or unclear rules. It can also point to cutting corners under pressure. You might note the facts calmly, seek appropriate support if needed, and check that your own actions match the standard you would like others to meet.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, Justice highlights integrity, fair process and careful decisions. It may reflect reviewing a contract of expectations, giving balanced feedback or weighing options on their merits. You might ask which choice you would be comfortable explaining openly to everyone affected.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Justice is imagined as a composed, upright figure holding balanced scales at heart height and an upright blade pointing to the sky. The figure looks straight at the viewer, suggesting honesty with nothing hidden. Two simple columns and a plain curtain behind keep the scene uncluttered, as if clearing space for careful thought. Cool air-blues and a single warm accent may reflect the meeting of reason and conscience.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, Justice may reflect a sense that something is unfair, or that the scales in a situation have tipped. You might feel you are carrying more than your share, or notice a temptation to avoid looking at your own part in a difficulty.
This card can also point to judging yourself too harshly, weighing every choice against an impossible standard. Accountability is useful; constant self-criticism is not the same thing.
You may want to write down the situation as neutrally as you can, as if explaining it to a fair-minded friend. What is yours to own, and what is not? Seeking fairness might mean speaking up, making a repair, or simply letting go of a judgment that has become heavy to carry.
cards.meaningUpright:
Justice holds a set of scales in one hand and a sword in the other. The scales stand for weighing things carefully; the sword for the clarity to act once you have. This card is about fairness, honesty and taking responsibility for your choices, understanding that actions have consequences and that you can choose them with care.
In everyday life this card may reflect a decision that needs a clear head, such as dividing tasks fairly, giving honest feedback or admitting a mistake and making amends. It can point to moments when you are asked to look at a situation from every side before responding, and to be as fair to yourself as you try to be to others.
This card invites you to consider what a balanced response would look like. You might ask which facts matter, what each person involved needs, and what you can take responsibility for. Justice does not predict how any formal matter will turn out. It highlights integrity: acting in line with what you believe is right, and accepting what follows with a steady mind.
cards.name: Justice
reflectionQuestions: What would a fair response look like here, to others and to yourself?
Where might responsibilities in a close relationship need rebalancing?
What is one thing you are ready to take ownership of this week?
cards.shortReversed: Something may feel out of balance. This card invites you to look at it clearly, including your own part.
cards.shortUpright: A moment to weigh things honestly and act in a way you would feel good explaining later.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Hanged Man may ask whether you are avoiding stillness or stuck in it. It can reflect restlessness or a sense of being on hold. You might check in with yourself: is this a time for patience, or a time for a gentle push? Your honest answer can guide the next step.
aspects.growthUpright: Letting go is a skill, and the Hanged Man offers a chance to practice it. What you release might be a belief, an expectation or a habit of rushing. You might try doing one familiar thing in reverse order or from a new angle, and notice what that small disruption reveals about how you usually see the world.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to a relationship in limbo, with neither person naming what they want. It can also reflect giving more than feels fair in the hope that things will change. You might consider whether it is time to say gently what you need, so that both of you can move forward.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Hanged Man can reflect a moment to step back and see a situation from the other person's point of view. It may invite you to let go of needing to win an argument or to fix everything right now. Patience and a willingness to see differently can open unexpected understanding.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the Hanged Man may reflect a project stuck for too long or a decision endlessly postponed. You might ask what information or support you are really waiting for. Setting a gentle deadline for yourself, or choosing to let one option go, can help movement return.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the Hanged Man highlights a pause for rethinking. Delays can be frustrating, yet they may offer time to question assumptions, research alternatives or let an idea mature. You might use a slow period to look at your work from a completely different angle.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Hanged Man is imagined suspended upside down by one ankle from a sturdy, living branch, arms relaxed and face calm, even curious. From this angle the figure sees the world reflected in a pool below, turned the other way round. The tree is green and in bud, showing that the pause is part of growth rather than an end to it. Watery blues and loose, flowing clothing echo surrender, dreaming and seeing beneath the surface.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Hanged Man may reflect a pause that has lasted beyond its purpose. You might feel stuck in limbo, waiting for something to change without quite knowing what you are waiting for. Indecision can start to feel safer than choosing.
This card can also point to resisting a pause you need, filling every moment to avoid the discomfort of stillness, or sacrificing your own needs in a way that no longer serves anyone.
You may want to ask what the waiting is protecting. If it is time to move, what is the smallest step that would get you unstuck? If you need to stop, what permission could you give yourself to rest without guilt? Either way, the choice is yours to make, and making it can restore a sense of direction.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Hanged Man hangs upside down from a living tree, yet the face is calm, sometimes even glowing. This is not a card of punishment. It is a card of deliberate suspension: stepping out of the usual flow of doing in order to see things differently. When you turn the world upside down, what looked obvious can suddenly look strange, and what seemed impossible can come within reach.
In everyday life this card may reflect a project on hold, a plan delayed by circumstances, or a moment when you realize that pushing harder is not helping. It can point to the value of letting go of a fixed idea about how something should unfold. Sometimes the most useful move is to stop moving and simply look.
This card invites you to consider what a pause might be offering you. You might ask what you would notice if you looked at your situation from the opposite angle. The Hanged Man suggests that surrender, in the sense of releasing the need to control, can make room for insight, and that waiting can be active when it is paired with attention.
cards.name: The Hanged Man
reflectionQuestions: What might you see if you looked at your situation from the opposite side?
Where are you waiting for someone else to move first?
What could you let go of this week to make room for something new?
cards.shortReversed: Waiting may have turned into stalling. What would help you decide whether to stay still or move?
cards.shortUpright: A pause, chosen or not, can offer a view you would never see while rushing ahead.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, Death may ask whether fear of change is keeping you in a smaller space than you need. It can reflect a slow, patient transformation that deserves your trust. You might choose one small thing to let go of this week and notice how it feels afterward.
aspects.growthUpright: Old identities can fall away like leaves, making room for what is still forming. You might notice beliefs about yourself that were true once but are not true now. Releasing them can create room for a version of you that is more honest to who you are becoming.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to holding on to an old dynamic that both people have outgrown, or to difficulty accepting that a connection has changed. You might consider what you would need to let the relationship take its new shape, whatever that shape turns out to be.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card can reflect a significant change in how a bond works: a new stage, a shift in roles, or the end of a pattern that no longer helped either person. It does not point to anyone's physical wellbeing. It may invite you to acknowledge what is changing together, with honesty and care.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, Death may reflect staying with a task, role or method out of habit after it has stopped fitting. It can also point to fear of what comes after. You might list what the current situation still gives you and what it costs, and notice what the balance tells you.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, Death highlights completion and transition. It may reflect finishing a role, closing a project or retiring a way of working that has run its course. You might take stock of what you have learned and what you want to carry forward into the next chapter.

cards.imageryNote: Taro's Death is imagined as a quiet autumn landscape where a slow river carries fallen leaves toward a rising sun on the horizon. A cloaked, unhurried figure walks beside the water, carrying a single seed pod or bare branch, symbols of what ends and what waits to grow. A white flower on a dark background can suggest renewal within release. The mood is calm and respectful, pointing to transformation rather than loss.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, Death may reflect an ending that is taking its time. You might sense that a phase is over while still holding on to it, perhaps because the familiar feels safer than the unknown, or because letting go feels like losing part of yourself.
This card can also point to a transition happening slowly and quietly, below the surface, rather than in one clear moment. Not every change arrives with a clean break.
You may want to notice what you are clinging to and what the clinging is protecting.
