cards.shortUpright: You have come through a lot and are still standing; this card honors your resilience on the final stretch.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, you may be discovering the lightness that comes from putting something down. You might explore what you want to keep carrying because it gives meaning, and what you are ready to release. Choosing your responsibilities, rather than simply accepting them, can be a quiet act of self-respect.
aspects.growthUpright: A useful belief to question here is that you must handle everything yourself. Where did that belief come from? You might notice how your body and mood respond to a heavy load, and treat those signals as information about what needs to change.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, you may be learning to ask for help or to step back from roles you took on for others. This can feel uncomfortable at first. You might consider which responsibilities you would like to share and how to ask in a way that invites cooperation, rather than waiting until you are too tired to ask at all.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect an imbalance in who carries what: one person handling most of the planning, the worrying or the emotional work. You might notice whether the load feels fair and talk about it openly. Sharing the weight can bring people closer, while silent overcarrying often breeds quiet resentment.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, you may be starting to set boundaries, delegate or renegotiate deadlines, or you may be resisting doing so. You might identify one task that someone else could handle, or one commitment you could decline. Making space in your workload can restore both focus and the enthusiasm that started the work.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in study, the Ten of Wands can point to overcommitment: more tasks than time, or a project that has grown beyond its first shape. You might take stock of your commitments, clarify priorities with the people involved, and look for anything that can be simplified. Finishing well often depends on carrying less at once.

cards.imageryNote: A figure walks bent forward, arms wrapped around a tall bundle of ten staffs that nearly hides their face, heading toward a small house or town on the horizon. The bundle stands for accumulated responsibilities, the hidden face for the way a heavy load can narrow one's view, and the nearby destination for an end that is within reach. The open road leaves room to imagine the load being shared or set down.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Ten of Wands can point to a moment of release. You may be starting to put down responsibilities that were never yours, to delegate, or to say no to requests that would add more weight. There can be relief in realizing you do not have to carry everything at once.
It can also reflect the opposite pattern turned inward: insisting on doing it all alone, even when help is available, because asking feels harder than struggling.
This may be a good time to sort your load. You might list what you are carrying and mark what could be shared, postponed or dropped. Small changes, such as one delegated task or one declined invitation, can make a real difference. Letting go is not failing; it can be a way of keeping your energy for what matters most.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Ten of Wands shows someone carrying a large bundle of staffs, arms wrapped around them, head bent, walking toward a house in the distance. The fire that began as a single spark has multiplied into many commitments, and each one takes effort to hold.
This card often appears when responsibilities have piled up gradually: a project that kept growing, a role that absorbed extra tasks, looking after others while also trying to keep your own plans alive. Much of it may have started from enthusiasm or a sense of duty, and it can be hard to remember when it became so heavy.
This card invites you to look honestly at what you are holding. Which responsibilities are yours, and which have landed on you by default? Which ones still connect to something you care about? The destination may be close, but you might still ask whether you could carry this differently: in smaller loads, with help, or with some things set down along the way.
cards.name: Ten of Wands
reflectionQuestions: What are you carrying right now that may not be yours to carry?
Who could share part of this load if you asked them clearly?
What is one thing you could set down, postpone or decline this week?
cards.shortReversed: Some of the load may be ready to come off your shoulders; you could look at what you can put down, share or refuse.
cards.shortUpright: You may be carrying more than your share; this card invites you to notice the weight and what truly needs carrying.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, self-consciousness or a restless mind may be keeping you from going deeper. You might explore what it would mean to stay with one interest a little longer than feels natural, and to allow yourself to be visibly new at it. Depth often arrives just after the moment you would usually move on.
aspects.growthUpright: The Page of Wands hands you a simple assignment: reconnect with your curiosity. What did you love exploring when there was no pressure to achieve anything? You might set aside time for a playful experiment this week, and treat whatever you discover as useful information about what energizes you.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, excitement in a relationship may come in bursts and fade quickly, or you may feel shy about showing enthusiasm. You might notice whether you are looking for novelty rather than depth. Letting your genuine interest show, even in small ways, can invite the other person to respond with the same openness.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect fresh curiosity about someone: wanting to learn more about them, try new things together, or share playful energy. It can bring lightness to a familiar bond as well. You might ask someone close a question you have never asked, or suggest an activity neither of you has tried before.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, you may have many ideas and little follow-through, or feel unsure where to direct your energy. You might choose one project to carry one step further than usual. Talking with a mentor or colleague can also help turn a scattered spark into a clearer direction.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in study, the Page of Wands can point to a learning phase: a new skill, a fresh role, or an idea you are eager to test. Enthusiasm is an asset here. You might ask questions freely, volunteer for something unfamiliar, and treat early mistakes as part of the process rather than a verdict on your ability.

cards.imageryNote: A youthful figure stands in an open landscape, holding a staff upright and gazing at a fresh shoot sprouting from its wood with open fascination. Clothing can carry small flame or salamander motifs to hint at the element of fire. The sprouting staff stands for an idea that is alive and growing, the wondering gaze for curiosity, and the open land for the many directions still waiting to be explored.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Page of Wands can reflect curiosity that has nowhere to land. You may jump from one interest to another, starting projects with delight and dropping them when the novelty fades. Or the curiosity may be there but held back by worry about looking inexperienced.
This card can also describe ideas that are still forming: sparks that need more time before they are ready to share.
You might explore what is behind the restlessness or the hesitation. Is it boredom, fear of commitment, or fear of not being good enough yet? One way forward can be to pick a single interest and set a small, low-pressure goal for it. Another is to let yourself enjoy exploring without needing it to lead anywhere in particular.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Page of Wands is the eager student of fire. Holding a sprouting staff and looking at it with fascination, this figure represents curiosity before expertise: the joy of discovering something new and wanting to know more.
This energy can show up as signing up for a class on a whim, reading everything you can find about a new interest, or telling friends about an idea you have only just had. It may also be a message or invitation that opens a door to something unfamiliar. There is a sense of play here, and a willingness to be seen trying.
This card invites you to approach life with the openness of a beginner. You do not need to know where an interest leads to explore it. You might give yourself permission to experiment without pressure to be good at it straight away, and notice how that freedom feels. Sometimes the most lasting passions begin as small, playful questions.
cards.name: Page of Wands
reflectionQuestions: What are you curious about right now, even if it seems impractical?
Who in your life encourages you to try new things, and how could you spend time with them?
What small experiment could you start this week just to see what happens?
cards.shortReversed: Enthusiasm may be flickering between many things or held back by doubt; you might choose one to explore gently.
cards.shortUpright: A curious, playful energy wants to explore; follow what excites you and let yourself be a beginner.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, you might explore your relationship with impulse. When does spontaneity bring you joy, and when does it leave you scattered? Learning to pause briefly before acting, without losing your spark, can help your energy become something you steer rather than something that steers you.
aspects.growthUpright: Courage and an appetite for experience are gifts this card asks you to use. What would you do if you trusted your own enthusiasm? You might try something that stretches you, and notice how it feels to act from passion rather than only from caution.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, strong feelings may move faster than communication, or enthusiasm may cool as quickly as it arrived. You might notice whether you or someone close is acting on impulse without checking in. Slowing down to talk about what each person really wants can bring steadiness to a connection full of sparks.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect excitement, attraction and a sense of adventure: spontaneous plans, intense conversations, a desire to do things together. You might enjoy the energy while also checking that the pace suits everyone involved. Shared adventures tend to feel richer when both people have a say in the direction.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, you may be rushing decisions or feeling blocked and impatient. You might check whether speed is truly needed or whether a short pause for planning would serve you better. Turning frustration into a clear list of next actions can help your energy move forward instead of in circles.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the Knight of Wands can point to taking bold initiative: pitching an ambitious idea, leading a push, or moving quickly on an opportunity. You might use this drive to break through inertia, while making a simple plan for the steps after the first exciting burst.

cards.imageryNote: A rider in mid-gallop leans forward on a rearing or leaping horse, staff held high, cloak streaming behind. Desert hills or open plains stretch ahead, and small flame shapes or salamanders can decorate the rider's clothing. The leaping horse stands for passion and drive, the raised staff for purpose carried into action, and the wide landscape for adventure still unfolding. The forward lean hints at both courage and haste.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Knight of Wands can reflect energy that outruns its direction. You may start things in a rush and lose interest halfway, act on impulse and then have to deal with the consequences, or feel frustrated because your drive has nowhere to go.
It can also point to passion held back, with restlessness building because circumstances keep you waiting.
This may be a moment to ask where your fire wants to go and what would help it get there without burning out. You might pause before a big decision, finish one thing before starting the next, or find a healthy outlet for restless energy, such as movement, a creative task, or an honest conversation about what feels blocked.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Knight of Wands is fire in motion. Mounted on a spirited horse and holding a staff aloft, this figure charges ahead with passion, confidence and a taste for adventure. Where the Page wonders, the Knight acts.
This energy can appear as a sudden decision to travel, a surge of motivation to finally start that project, or a willingness to take a risk that would once have felt too bold. It can bring charm, courage and an infectious enthusiasm that draws others along.
This card invites you to trust your drive and let it carry you into new territory. Momentum is precious, and sometimes the only way to discover where a path leads is to set off. At the same time, a charging horse needs a rider who knows roughly where they are going. You might channel this energy into one clear adventure, and keep enough awareness to adjust if the ground changes beneath you.
cards.name: Knight of Wands
reflectionQuestions: Where do you feel a strong urge to move forward right now?
How might your enthusiasm affect the people around you, for better or for less?
What would help you aim your energy before you set off?
cards.shortReversed: Energy may be running ahead of direction; this could be a moment to slow the charge and choose where to aim.
cards.shortUpright: A bold, adventurous energy is ready to move; you might follow your passion while keeping an eye on the road.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, you might explore where self-doubt or comparison is taking up room in your thoughts. It can help to notice your own progress and qualities without measuring them against anyone else's. Rest and play are both ways of rekindling a fire that has burned low.
aspects.growthUpright: Your warmth has an effect on others, and this card asks you to own it. What makes you feel most alive and self-assured? You might notice the settings in which you feel confident and bring a little of that energy into areas where you usually hold back.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, you may feel overshadowed, taken for granted or tempted to compare yourself with others. You might consider whether you have been giving warmth without receiving it. Expressing what you need, and appreciating yourself before waiting for others to, can help restore balance in a close bond.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect warmth, openness and a strong sense of self within a bond. You might bring energy and encouragement to people you care about while staying true to your own needs. This quality can make relationships feel lively and honest, where each person is free to shine.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, you may be stretched across too many roles or doubting your abilities after a setback. You might identify the tasks that genuinely use your strengths and protect time for them. Stepping back from the need to be everywhere at once can help your natural confidence return.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in creative efforts, the Queen of Wands can point to confident leadership and a gift for inspiring others. You might take visible ownership of a project, share your ideas with conviction, and create an atmosphere where colleagues feel energized. Your enthusiasm can be a practical resource, not only a mood.

cards.imageryNote: A figure sits at ease on a broad seat set in a sunlit clearing, a leafing staff resting in one hand and the other open toward the viewer. A hearth fire glows beside them, and a watchful animal companion lies nearby. The hearth suggests warmth offered to others, the open hand generosity, and the relaxed posture a confidence that does not need to prove itself. Warm golds and ambers can echo fire at its most settled and radiant.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Queen of Wands can reflect a flame that has dimmed. You may be doubting yourself, feeling tired of always being the one who brings the energy, or holding back your vitality to avoid attention.
Sometimes the reversed Queen points to fire used in less generous ways: comparison, envy, or a need to control the spotlight. These often grow out of feeling unseen.
This may be a moment to tend your own fire. What has been draining your confidence, and what used to renew it? You might return to an activity that makes you feel alive, spend time with people who appreciate you, or rest without guilt. Confidence often comes back gradually, as you reconnect with what you care about rather than with how you appear.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Queen of Wands embodies fire that has become steady and radiant. Seated at ease beside a glowing hearth, a leafing staff in hand, this figure is confident without needing to prove anything. The energy here is warm, magnetic and generous: someone who can light up a room and still keep their own center.
You might recognize this quality in yourself when you speak up with ease, host people with genuine warmth, or pursue a creative project with both passion and practicality. It can also describe someone in your life whose confidence encourages others to shine.
This card invites you to own your gifts. Confidence does not have to be loud; it can be the calm sense that you have something worth offering. You might notice where you tend to shrink back and experiment with taking up a little more space. Sharing your warmth, enthusiasm and ideas can be a gift both to you and to the people around you.
cards.name: Queen of Wands
reflectionQuestions: Where do you feel most confident and fully yourself?
Whose warmth encourages you, and how could you offer that warmth to someone else?
What is one way you could take up a little more space this week?
cards.shortReversed: Your inner fire may be flickering or stretched thin; you could look at what drains your confidence and what renews it.
cards.shortUpright: A warm, confident energy is available to you; you might let yourself take up space and share your light with others.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, you might explore how you relate to control and patience. Do you feel you must always be in charge, or do you avoid leadership because it feels like too much? Finding a middle path, where you lead your own life with confidence and flexibility, can be a steady form of strength.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card invites you to take ownership of your direction. What do you want to build over the longer term, and what values guide it? You might write a short statement of purpose and use it as a reference point for the choices ahead.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, one person may be taking too much control of decisions, or impatience may be creating tension. You might notice whether you are listening fully to someone close or already planning your answer. Inviting the other person's ideas can turn a one-sided plan into a shared one.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect a confident, protective and encouraging presence. You might bring vision to shared plans and help those close to you believe in their own goals. The invitation is to lead with generosity, offering direction when it is welcome and support when someone else wants to steer.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, you may be pushing too hard, expecting others to match your pace, or feeling unsure of the direction yourself. You might step back to review the vision with the people involved. Asking for input and adjusting goals can make a plan both more realistic and more widely supported.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in a project, the King of Wands can point to leadership, strategic vision and the courage to take initiative. You might define a clear goal, communicate it with enthusiasm, and delegate in a way that trusts others' strengths. Integrity and consistency help people feel safe following an ambitious direction.

cards.imageryNote: A figure sits on a high seat at the edge of a lookout, leaning forward with a flowering staff planted firmly beside them, as if about to rise. Beyond them a road winds toward distant hills lit by late sun. The flowering staff suggests vision that is alive and growing, the lookout a wide view of what could be built, and the forward lean readiness to turn ideas into action. Embers or small flame motifs can carry the element of fire.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the King of Wands can reflect drive that has lost its balance. You may feel impatient with others' pace, push plans through without listening, or set goals so high that they leave no room for rest. On the other side, it can point to a leader, perhaps you, who has lost sight of the vision and feels unsure where to go next.
This card may be inviting you to look at how you use your influence. Is your energy inspiring people, or overwhelming them? Is the vision still alive for you?
You might pause to reconnect with your purpose, ask for honest feedback, or share decisions more widely. Strong leadership often grows from listening as much as from directing.
cards.meaningUpright:
The King of Wands brings the fire of the suit to maturity. Seated on a throne but leaning slightly forward, staff in hand, this figure looks ready to act. The energy is visionary and decisive: someone who can see where things could go and has the confidence and experience to set the direction.
This quality may show up when you take charge of a project, guide a group through a change, or make a bold decision grounded in clear values. It can also describe a mentor or leader whose sense of purpose gives others courage.
This card invites you to step into your own authority. Leadership here is less about control and more about vision, integrity and follow-through. You might ask what larger aim your current efforts serve and how you could share it clearly with the people involved. When a direction is honest and well communicated, others often want to join it rather than simply follow orders.
cards.name: King of Wands
reflectionQuestions: What vision are you working toward, and how clearly could you describe it to someone else?
How might you lead in a way that invites others to contribute their strengths?
Where could a little more patience make your drive more effective?
cards.shortReversed: Strong drive may be tipping into impatience or control; you might check whether your vision still leaves room for others.
cards.shortUpright: A clear, visionary energy invites you to lead with purpose and turn big ideas into a direction others can follow.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may suggest turning care inward before offering more outward. If your reserves feel low, you could treat rest and small pleasures as necessary rather than optional. It may help to notice what drains you and what refills you. If heavy feelings stay with you, talking with someone you trust can be a useful step too.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Ace of Cups invites emotional honesty with yourself. You might practice naming feelings as they arrive, without ranking them as good or bad. Journaling, time near water or simply pausing before you respond can make space for this. The aim is not constant happiness but a kinder, more open relationship with your inner life.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to affection that is held back, perhaps because of past hurt or plain tiredness. You might notice that you listen politely while staying slightly out of reach. There is no need to push. Consider whether one small, safe act of openness, like saying what you appreciate, could let a little more warmth move between you and someone close.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In close bonds, the Ace of Cups can reflect a fresh wave of warmth, whether with a partner, a friend, family or someone new. It may invite you to express affection simply and without calculation: a message sent because you thought of them, an honest thank-you, a moment of full attention. You might also notice how it feels to receive care as well as give it.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect work that has become mechanical, where you go through the motions while your interest waits somewhere else. This is common after long effort. You might ask what first drew you to this path, or which small part of it still feels alive, and see whether giving that part more room restores some of the flow.
aspects.workUpright: At work or in any project you care about, this card may reflect renewed enthusiasm, or a new idea that genuinely moves you. It can invite you to bring feeling into what you do: care for the people you serve, pleasure in the craft, curiosity about what could grow. You might note what excites you now, before practical concerns start to shape it.

cards.imageryNote: The art centers on a single vessel brimming over, its water falling in several thin streams into a still pool below. Water lilies or lotus leaves on the surface can stand for feelings that open slowly and root in deep places. A soft light above the cup may suggest receptivity, an offering held out rather than grasped. The overall mood is calm abundance: more than enough, spilling gently outward.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Ace of Cups may suggest that feeling is present but held close, like water in a covered jar. Perhaps you have been busy looking after others, or it has felt safer to keep emotions at arm's length for a while. There is nothing wrong with that; guarding your heart can be a sensible response to a demanding season.
This card can also reflect a sense of running on empty. You might notice that small pleasures land flatly, or that you are giving from a cup that has not been refilled in some time.
The invitation here is gentle. Rather than forcing yourself to feel more, you might look at what quietly restores you, such as sleep, a walk near water, an unhurried conversation or an hour when no one needs you. When something does refill the cup, let yourself notice it. Openness can return at its own pace.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Ace of Cups is the first stirring of the suit of water: a single vessel so full that it spills over. It can reflect a feeling that arrives before you have words for it, such as tenderness, awe, relief or a sudden warmth toward someone or something. Nothing has to be done with it yet. The card simply asks you to notice that it is there.
In everyday life this might look like laughing properly for the first time in weeks, feeling moved by a piece of music, or finding that an old resentment has softened without you trying. It can also point to a new creative impulse, or a wish to be kinder to yourself.
This card invites you to stay open rather than manage the feeling straight away. You might ask where your care wants to go, and whether you are letting some of it reach you too. An open heart is not a promise of anything; it is a way of meeting the day with a little more room inside.
cards.name: Ace of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What feeling has been trying to get your attention lately?
Who or what has refilled your cup recently, and how might you thank them?
What is one small way you could let more warmth in this week?
cards.shortReversed: Your cup may need filling before it can pour; consider what would quietly replenish you today.
cards.shortUpright: A fresh feeling may be rising; this card invites you to let it in and notice where it wants to flow.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask whether you rely on others for a sense of balance you could also build inside. You might notice where you seek approval before trusting your own view. Treating yourself with the same fairness you offer a close friend can be a steadying practice, one small choice at a time.
aspects.growthUpright: Inner partnership is the growth theme here, a chance to reconcile parts of yourself: what you want and what you value, or your practical side and your tender one. You might write a short dialogue between two voices inside you and see where they already agree. Integration can feel like finding a partner within.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may reflect a bond where one person carries more of the emotional weight, or where a misunderstanding has not been cleared. You might consider what you would say if you knew it would be heard kindly. Repair often starts with one honest sentence and a willingness to hear the reply without defending yourself straight away.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card can reflect mutual attraction, friendship or a partnership where both people feel seen. It may invite you to notice the small rituals that keep a bond steady: checking in, remembering what matters to the other person, apologizing simply. You might ask what you appreciate most about someone close, and whether they know it.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect a working relationship where expectations are unspoken or uneven. Perhaps one person assumes agreement where there is none. You might name what you each expect, in plain words, and check whether your roles still fit. Clarity can be a kindness, even when the conversation feels awkward at first.
aspects.workUpright: At work, the Two of Cups can point to a promising collaboration, a colleague you trust or a client relationship built on respect. It may invite you to share credit, ask for input and make agreements clear enough that both sides feel secure. Good partnerships often grow from shared values more than from shared skills.

cards.imageryNote: The art pairs two figures, or two hands, each raising a cup toward the other across a small space. Between them, a shared emblem such as intertwined stems or twin fish can suggest that the meeting creates something neither holds alone. Mirrored colors on each side may express equality, with a gentle glow where the cups nearly touch, as if the connection itself gives off light.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Two of Cups may point to a connection that has tipped out of balance. One person may be giving more, or listening less, or two people may simply be talking past each other. It does not have to mean anything is broken; many bonds go through seasons like this.
The card can also turn inward, asking how well you partner with yourself. Are you as patient and fair with your own needs as you try to be with someone else's?
You might look at a relationship that feels uneven and ask what each person is really hoping for, beneath the surface disagreement. A calm, honest conversation, or a little distance to see more clearly, may be more useful than trying to fix everything at once. Balance is something people build together, one exchange at a time.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Two of Cups shows two people, or two parts of a life, meeting as equals and offering something to each other. It is a card of recognition: the relief of being understood, and the pleasure of understanding someone in return. The connection it describes can be romantic, but it can just as easily be a friendship, a creative collaboration, a sibling bond or a working partnership.
You might recognize this energy in a conversation where both people listen, in a reconciliation after a misunderstanding, or in the quiet agreement of two people who choose to keep showing up for each other. It can also reflect bringing together two sides of yourself that have been pulling in different directions.
This card invites you to notice where there is genuine give and take in your life, and to honor it. Reciprocity does not mean keeping score. It means both people feel free to offer, to receive and to say what they need.
cards.name: Two of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What makes you feel truly met by another person?
Where does a connection in your life feel uneven, and what might restore some balance?
How could you show appreciation to someone who keeps showing up for you?
cards.shortReversed: Something between you and another may feel out of balance; consider what each of you is really asking for.
cards.shortUpright: A moment to notice where care flows both ways, and what makes a connection feel equal and alive.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask whether you are using busyness or company to avoid being alone with your thoughts. It could also reflect loneliness that is hard to admit. You might balance social time with solitude and notice which one you are missing more. Reaching out to one person can be a gentle place to start.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, this card invites you to value joy as part of a balanced life, not a reward you must earn first. You might keep a note of small shared delights across a week. Noticing them can make it easier to recognize the community you already have, and to see where you might like to widen it.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may reflect tension in a group, or a sense of being left out. It can also point to an outside influence on a bond, in whatever form it takes. Rather than guessing, you might ask plainly how things stand. It may also help to spend time with people around whom you do not have to perform or keep up.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card highlights the wider web around a bond: friends, family, chosen family. It may invite you to share good moments with the people who support you, or to welcome someone close into your circle. You might also notice how much your friendships sustain you, and give them some of the attention usually reserved for a single relationship.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect a team that has lost its warmth, perhaps through gossip, cliques or simple overload. You might notice whether social pressure is shaping your choices, such as staying late to fit in. Consider what healthy collegiality would look like for you, and where you could model it in a small way.
aspects.workUpright: At work, the Three of Cups can point to team spirit, a shared win or collaborators who genuinely enjoy working together. It may invite you to celebrate progress along the way, not only at the finish. Thanking people by name, sharing credit and marking small milestones can make a group stronger and the work more satisfying.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows three figures in a loose circle, their cups lifted and meeting in the middle. Around their feet, a harvest of fruit, flowers or vines can suggest abundance that grows from shared effort. Their different clothing, postures and colors may stand for friends who stay distinct while belonging together. Movement in the scene, like a dance step or a turning hem, conveys easy, unforced joy.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Three of Cups may reflect a social life that feels out of tune. You might feel on the edge of a group you once felt part of, or notice that friendships have drifted as lives changed. Alternatively, there may be too much of a good thing: plans that leave no room to rest, or celebrations that have become a way to avoid quieter feelings.
None of this is a verdict on your friendships. Circles change shape, and it is natural to outgrow some gatherings and long for others.
The invitation is to look at the quality of your connections rather than their number. Which people leave you feeling more like yourself? Where might you be saying yes out of habit? A single honest catch-up with one friend may offer more than a crowded calendar.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Three of Cups is a card of friends raising their cups together. It celebrates the kind of connection that does not need a reason: laughter at a kitchen table, a group chat that lights up with good news, neighbors who help without being asked. Where the Two of Cups looks at one bond, this card looks at the circle.
It can reflect a season of gatherings, a milestone worth marking or simply a sense of belonging to a group that sees you. It might also point to support that is already around you, perhaps more than you have been noticing.
This card invites you to let joy be shared rather than saved for later. You might reach out to someone you have been meaning to see, say yes to an invitation or create a small occasion of your own. Celebration does not need to be grand. Sometimes it is just acknowledging, together, that something good happened, or that you got through something hard.
cards.name: Three of Cups
reflectionQuestions: Who are the people you most want to celebrate with, and why?
Which gatherings leave you feeling full, and which leave you feeling drained?
What small occasion could you create to share something good this week?
cards.shortReversed: Connection may feel thin or tiring right now; consider which gatherings nourish you and which only fill time.
cards.shortUpright: A moment to notice who shares your joys, and how you might share theirs in return.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may reflect coming out of a reflective period with clearer priorities. You might notice gratitude returning for things you once took for granted. It could help to write down what you learned while you were withdrawn, so the insight stays with you as life gets busier again.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Four of Cups invites honest reflection on what truly satisfies you. You might list the things you do out of habit and ask which of them still matter. Quiet time can be valuable, as long as it remains a choice rather than a place where you feel stuck.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may suggest reconnecting after a withdrawn stretch. You might feel more willing to hear what someone has been trying to say, or to reach out first. If you still need space, saying so kindly can protect the bond. Small shared moments, like a walk or a meal, can be a comfortable way to find your way back.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Four of Cups may reflect a need for space, or a sense that a bond has become routine. It can invite you to ask whether you are overlooking care that is being offered, such as a gesture, a question or an invitation. You might tell someone close that you need time to think, so that distance is not mistaken for disinterest.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may point to motivation returning, or to a readiness to say yes to something new. You might notice which projects have begun to interest you again. If you feel stuck in a loop of declining, consider trying one small commitment and reflecting afterwards on whether it gave you energy or took it.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect restlessness, a sense that tasks no longer mean much, or a pause to reassess direction. It may invite you to look again at opportunities you dismissed quickly. A conversation, a new responsibility or a course you ignored could be worth a second look, even if the spark is not there yet.

cards.imageryNote: The art places a seated figure beneath a tree or beside still water, arms folded, gaze lowered toward three cups on the ground. A fourth cup drifts toward them on a breeze or floats on the water's surface, easy to miss. Muted colors and a closed posture can suggest inwardness and a need for pause, while the offered cup keeps a thread of possibility in view.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Four of Cups may reflect a turning point after a period of withdrawal. You might feel ready to look up again, open to conversations and possibilities that seemed dull or out of reach before. Curiosity can return quietly, first as restlessness, then as interest.
It can also point the other way: a withdrawal that has lasted longer than it helped, becoming a habit of saying no. You might notice whether you are declining invitations from real need or simply from inertia.
Either way, this card invites a gentle check-in. What, if anything, has started to catch your attention again? You do not have to accept every offer that arrives. Choosing one small thing to engage with, and seeing how it feels, may be enough to learn what you are ready for now.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Four of Cups often shows a figure sitting apart, looking at three cups in front of them while a fourth is offered, perhaps unnoticed. It is a card of pause and inner weighing. Something that once satisfied you may have lost its taste, and you are not yet sure what would replace it.
This can look like boredom with a routine, a flat feeling after reaching a goal, or a wish to step back from social life for a while. It can also be genuine contemplation: taking time to consider what you want before saying yes to anything else.
Withdrawal is not a failure. Sometimes it is exactly what a tired heart needs. The card simply invites you to stay curious rather than closed. While you sit with your thoughts, you might glance up now and then and notice what is being held out to you. An offer of help, a new idea or a small kindness may be closer than it seems, and you are free to decide whether it fits.
cards.name: Four of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What has lost its appeal for you lately, and what might that be telling you?
What might someone be offering you that you have not fully noticed?
What is one small invitation you could say yes to, just to see how it feels?
cards.shortReversed: Interest may be returning after a quiet stretch; consider which invitation feels worth accepting now.
cards.shortUpright: You may be turned inward for a while; this card invites you to notice what is being offered while you reflect.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, the Five of Cups may reflect resilience growing after a hard time. You might notice a new perspective or a deeper compassion that the experience gave you. Marking the change with a small ritual, like writing a letter you do not send, can help you close one chapter and open the next.
aspects.growthUpright: Grief and regret deserve a place in your story, and this card asks how to give them that place without letting them write the rest of it. You might practice noticing when your attention returns again and again to what went wrong. Gently widening the view, even for a few minutes each day, can make it easier to see the whole picture.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect movement toward reconciliation, or toward peace with how a relationship has changed. You might be ready to let go of an old grievance, or at least hold it more loosely. Consider what forgiveness would look like for you, remembering that it does not require you to accept what does not feel right.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect sadness over a bond that has changed, a hope that was not met or words that hurt. It can invite you to acknowledge that feeling rather than brushing it aside. You might also notice the people who have stayed close through difficulty, and let them know how much that means to you.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect recovering from a setback and starting to see new options. You might notice that a door you mourned closing has left space for something else. Consider writing a brief review of what happened, focusing on lessons rather than blame, so you can move on with more clarity.
aspects.workUpright: At work, the Five of Cups can reflect disappointment over a project that stalled, feedback that stung or an opportunity that went elsewhere. It may invite you to take a moment to process that before planning the next step. Afterward, you might list the skills, relationships and ideas that are still yours to build on.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows a cloaked figure with head bowed over three toppled cups, their contents seeping into the ground. Behind the figure, two cups remain upright and easy to overlook. A path or a crossing in the distance can suggest a way onward when the time is right. Cool, subdued tones express mourning, while a thin line of light on the standing cups hints that not everything is gone.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Five of Cups may reflect a slow return of steadiness after a disappointment. You might notice that the loss hurts less sharply, or that you can speak about it without it filling the whole day. Acceptance does not mean pretending it did not matter; it means finding room to carry it alongside other things.
This card can also point to forgiveness, of someone else or of yourself, becoming a little more possible. Or it can suggest that grief has been set aside rather than felt, and is asking for a quieter moment of attention.
You might ask what you have learned from this experience and what you want to take forward. Turning toward what remains is not a betrayal of what was lost. If heavy feelings stay with you, sharing them with someone you trust can make the load feel lighter.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Five of Cups shows a figure looking down at cups that have spilled, while others remain upright behind them. It is a card about disappointment and grief: the feeling of something not turning out as hoped, and the pull to stay with what has been lost.
That pull is human. When a plan falls through, a friendship changes or an expectation is not met, it takes time to absorb it. This card does not ask you to hurry. Mourning is part of caring about something, and naming a loss can be a way of honoring it.
In everyday life, this card might reflect replaying a conversation, going over what you could have done differently, or finding it hard to enjoy something because of what is missing. It gently invites you, when you are ready, to turn slightly and notice what has not spilled: relationships, strengths or options that are still there. Both things can be true at once, the loss and what remains.
cards.name: Five of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What loss or disappointment is asking to be acknowledged right now?
Who or what has stayed with you through a difficult time?
What still stands in your life that you could turn toward, even briefly?
cards.shortReversed: The weight of a disappointment may be easing; consider what has remained with you and where you want to turn next.
cards.shortUpright: A loss may be filling your view; this card invites you to grieve honestly and, in time, notice what still stands.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask you to update an old story about yourself. Perhaps a label from childhood still shapes how you see your abilities. You might write down one belief from the past and ask whether it is still true. Letting it go can make room for who you are becoming.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Six of Cups invites you to reconnect with the curiosity and delight of your younger self. You might revisit an activity you loved as a child, with no goal but enjoyment. Remembering what once made you feel light and unhurried can guide choices about how you spend your time now.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to a bond held together mainly by the past, or to comparing someone with who they used to be. You might consider whether you are relating to the person in front of you now, or to an older picture of them. Letting each other change can keep a connection alive and honest.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Six of Cups may reflect a reunion, a shared memory or a friendship with deep roots. It can invite playfulness and simple gestures, such as a note, a shared snack or an old photo sent with a smile. You might notice how shared history creates trust, and how you could add new memories together.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect clinging to how things used to be done, or resisting a change because the old way feels safer. You might ask which traditions still serve the work and which are kept out of habit. Respecting the past while making room for new approaches can ease a transition for everyone.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect returning to something you enjoyed early on, mentoring someone newer or drawing on old skills in a fresh way. It may invite you to bring simple goodwill into the workplace. Small courtesies, like offering help before you are asked, often shape a culture more than big statements do.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows two small figures in a sheltered courtyard or garden, one offering a cup filled with flowers to the other. Other cups nearby, each holding blossoms, suggest memories planted and still growing. An old wall or a doorway in the background can stand for home and the protection of familiar places. Warm, soft colors convey innocence, generosity and the easy trust of earlier days.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Six of Cups may suggest that memory has become a place to hide rather than a place to visit. You might find yourself comparing the present unfavorably with an idealized version of the past, or holding onto old patterns and roles that no longer fit.
It can also point the other way: a readiness to grow beyond something from your history, leaving an old story behind so a new one can begin.
This card invites you to look at the past with kindness and honesty together. What really happened, and what have you added in remembering it? You might keep the parts that nourish you and loosen your grip on those that keep you small. Growing up does not mean losing tenderness; it can mean bringing it with you into choices that belong to today.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Six of Cups is a card of memory and gentle kindness. It often shows one figure offering a cup of flowers to another, a gesture that is simple, generous and free of calculation. It can bring to mind childhood, old friends, familiar places or a time when things felt easier.
In daily life, this card might reflect reconnecting with someone from your past, returning to a hobby you once loved, or finding comfort in a song, a recipe or a smell that carries you back. It can also point to small acts of kindness given and received without expectation.
The invitation is to let the past offer what it can: warmth, perspective, a reminder of who you have always been. Nostalgia can be a resource when it helps you remember what matters to you. You might ask which quality from an earlier time you would like to bring into the present, such as playfulness, curiosity or ease.
cards.name: Six of Cups
reflectionQuestions: Which memory brings you comfort, and what does it remind you to value?
Who from your past would you like to reconnect with, and why?
What part of an old story about yourself might be ready to change?
cards.shortReversed: The past may be pulling harder than usual; consider which memories nourish you and which keep you from the present.
cards.shortUpright: A memory or a simple kindness may bring warmth today; this card invites you to notice what the past still gives you.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may reflect a growing ability to tell wishes apart from intentions. You might practice making one clear decision each day, however small. Over time, this can build trust in your own judgment while leaving room for imagination to inspire rather than distract.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Seven of Cups invites you to understand your daydreams. What longing does each one express? You might journal about a recurring fantasy and look for the need beneath it, such as freedom, recognition or rest. Meeting that need in a small, real way can be more satisfying than the dream itself.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, the Seven of Cups may point to seeing a relationship more clearly, perhaps after a romantic haze has lifted. This clarity can be a chance to build on what is real. You might ask what you truly value in the bond now, rather than what you pictured at the start, and share that openly.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect idealizing someone, or imagining many possible futures with or without a particular person. It can invite you to notice the difference between who someone is and who you hope they are. You might enjoy the imagination while grounding it in real conversations about what each of you wants.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect narrowing down to a clear direction, or finally committing to one project. You might notice a sense of focus returning. If you feel disillusioned, consider which parts of the original vision are still worth carrying forward into something more realistic and more your own.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect a surplus of ideas or options, such as several projects, paths or offers competing for attention. It may invite you to weigh each one against your priorities, time and energy. Writing them down side by side can help. Imagination is useful for brainstorming; decisions often need firmer ground.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows a figure, seen from behind, facing seven cups that hover in drifting mist. Each cup holds a different symbol, perhaps a key, a garland, a small house, a star, a coiled shape, a closed box and a mirror, standing for access, praise, security, hope, unease, secrets and self-image. Soft, dreamlike light and shifting colors can suggest how alluring and uncertain these visions are, inviting the viewer to wonder which of them is real.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Seven of Cups may reflect clarity arriving after a period of confusion. The floating cups may start to settle, and you might see which ones hold something substantial and which were mostly mist. This can feel like relief, or like a small disappointment as some fantasies fade.
It can also suggest the opposite: avoiding choice by keeping every possibility open, or dismissing imagination entirely in the name of being practical.
The invitation here is to find grounded middle ground. You might pick one option and test it in a small, low-pressure way. Notice what excites you in practice rather than in theory. Letting go of a daydream can open room for a plan you can actually live, and dreaming can remain something you return to for inspiration.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Seven of Cups often shows a figure facing a row of cups that float in the air, each holding a different vision. It is a card of imagination, possibility and the dizziness that can come from having too many choices.
Imagination is a gift. It lets you picture lives you have not lived yet and ideas no one else has had. But this card also notices how easily daydreams blur with plans. Some of the cups hold real opportunities, some hold wishes, and some hold worries dressed up as possibilities.
In everyday life, this might look like jumping between projects, scrolling through options without choosing, or feeling pulled toward a dream that has no first step. The card invites you to enjoy dreaming and then to look more closely. Which option fits your values and your actual circumstances? What would the first small action be? Choosing one does not mean losing the others forever; it means giving something the chance to become real.
cards.name: Seven of Cups
reflectionQuestions: Which of your current options feels most alive when you imagine taking a real step toward it?
What longing might be hiding beneath a daydream you keep returning to?
What one small choice could you make this week to move from imagining to doing?
cards.shortReversed: The fog of options may be lifting; consider which choice still feels real once the glow of imagining fades.
cards.shortUpright: Many possibilities may be shimmering at once; this card invites you to enjoy imagining, then look closely at each one.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask you to notice patterns of avoidance or restlessness. Are you leaving situations to escape discomfort, or staying to avoid change? You might practice sitting with uncertainty a little longer before acting. Understanding your own pattern can make future choices clearer and kinder.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Eight of Cups invites a journey inward. You might set aside time to reflect on what gives your life meaning now, as opposed to what did before. Walking, journaling or a short break from routine can help you hear what you are ready to move toward.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, the Eight of Cups may reflect hesitation about a relationship that feels unfulfilling, or a pattern of withdrawing whenever closeness grows. You might ask whether you are staying from love or from fear, and whether you are leaving from need or from habit. Clear, kind communication can help either way.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect a wish for more depth, or a recognition that a bond has run its course in its current form. It can invite honest reflection on what you need that is missing. Stepping back might mean a conversation about change, more personal space or, sometimes, choosing a different kind of connection.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect feeling stuck in a job or project you have outgrown, or jumping between roles without settling. You might list what you would miss and what you would gladly leave. Consider whether a change of approach, rather than a change of place, could meet the need you are feeling.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect a desire for more purpose, even when everything looks stable. It may invite you to explore what would feel more meaningful, perhaps by trying a new area, learning something different or reshaping your current role. Moving on can be an inner shift long before it becomes an outer one.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows a lone figure with a walking staff, seen from behind as they leave a careful stack of cups on the shore. Ahead lie rising hills and a winding path under a thin crescent moon. A visible gap in the stacked cups can suggest something incomplete. Deep blues and silvers evoke introspection and the quiet pull toward what has not yet been explored.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Eight of Cups may reflect being caught between staying and leaving. You might sense that something is not right but feel unsure whether to move on or try again. Fear of the unknown, or loyalty to what you have built, can keep you in place.
It can also point to the opposite pattern: leaving again and again, drifting from one thing to the next without giving anything the chance to deepen.
This card invites you to slow down and look at the choice more closely. What would staying look like if it were chosen rather than defaulted to? What would leaving require? You might talk it through with someone you trust, or set a gentle deadline for deciding. Whichever direction you choose, making the choice deliberately can bring a sense of peace.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Eight of Cups often shows a figure walking away from a neat row of cups, heading toward open ground under a night sky. The cups are not broken or spilled. It is simply that something about them no longer satisfies, and the figure has decided to look for what is missing.
This card speaks to the quiet courage of leaving something that seems fine from the outside: a role, a routine, an identity or a way of living that has stopped feeling true. It is often less a dramatic exit than a slow recognition that you have outgrown something.
In daily life, it may reflect wanting more meaning from your work, needing time alone to think, or stepping back from a situation that drains you. The card invites you to take that longing seriously. Walking away does not have to be sudden or permanent; it can be a trial distance, a pause of the mind. You might ask what you are really searching for, and what you are willing to leave behind to find it.
cards.name: Eight of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What in your life looks complete but no longer feels fulfilling?
What are you searching for that your current situation does not offer?
What small step could help you explore a change without committing to it yet?
cards.shortReversed: You may be torn between staying and going; consider what you would need to know before choosing either one.
cards.shortUpright: Something may no longer fill you, even if it looks complete; this card invites you to notice where your heart is pulling next.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask you to examine the difference between pleasure and fulfillment. You might notice habits of consumption, busyness or comparison that leave you wanting more. Exploring what brings deep satisfaction, rather than a quick lift, can guide gentler and more lasting choices.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Nine of Cups invites a practice of gratitude and enjoyment. You might end each day by noting three things that felt good, however small. Over time, this can train your attention toward contentment and make it easier to recognize when you have enough.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to expecting a relationship to supply all your contentment, or to feeling that something is missing despite outward harmony. You might explore which needs you could meet for yourself, and what you would like to ask for more openly from someone close.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Nine of Cups may reflect feeling content and at ease with the people around you. It can invite you to enjoy a connection as it is, sharing pleasures and saying what you appreciate. You might notice what a satisfying bond looks like for you, so you can nurture it with intention rather than by chance.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect success that feels hollow, or chasing markers of achievement that do not reflect what you value. You might ask what would make your work feel meaningful, not just impressive. Aligning goals with your values can turn accomplishment into genuine satisfaction.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect satisfaction with an achievement, recognition for effort or simply enjoying what you do. It may invite you to pause and acknowledge the progress you have made. Celebrating a milestone, even privately, can restore energy for whatever comes next and remind you why the work matters.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows a figure seated at ease, shoulders relaxed, with nine full cups set around them on low tables and cushions, like a room prepared for guests. Their open, satisfied expression suggests pleasure and self-assurance. Rich but warm colors, perhaps deep reds and golds, can evoke comfort and hospitality, a gentle reminder of a hope that has found some form.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Nine of Cups may reflect a gap between how things look and how they feel. You might have what you thought you wanted and still sense something missing. Or pleasure may have tipped into excess, with comfort becoming a way to avoid feelings rather than enjoy life.
It can also turn inward, suggesting that lasting contentment is less about possessions or achievements and more about your relationship with yourself.
This card invites honest reflection. What did you expect this wish to bring, and what did it actually bring? You might look for satisfaction in values, connection and meaning as well as in results. Small, sincere pleasures, chosen with care, may offer more than accumulating more. It is fine to want things; the question is what would feel like enough.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Nine of Cups is often called the wish card. It shows a figure at ease among full cups, clearly pleased with what they have. It speaks to contentment: the feeling of enough, of a wish met or a hope that came to something.
This card invites you to notice satisfaction when it is present, instead of moving straight to the next goal. Perhaps you finished something you worked hard on, enjoyed a good meal with people you like, or simply feel at ease in your life for a moment. These experiences are worth savoring.
It can also invite you to reflect on what you truly wish for. If you could pour one more cup, what would it hold? Knowing your wishes clearly can shape choices in small, practical ways. Enjoying pleasure and comfort is part of a full life. Gratitude, in this sense, is not about feeling you should be happy; it is about noticing what is already good and letting it count.
cards.name: Nine of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What in your life right now feels like enough?
Which wish have you been holding, and what do you hope it would bring you?
How could you savor something good this week without rushing to the next goal?
cards.shortReversed: Something may look satisfying without feeling so; consider what would bring you contentment from the inside.
cards.shortUpright: A moment to savor what is already good, and to notice how much of it you helped bring about.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask you to examine beliefs about what a happy life should look like. You might find that some expectations come from others rather than from you. Letting go of an idealized image can make room for a more authentic and more livable sense of fulfillment.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Ten of Cups invites you to cultivate a sense of home within yourself. You might notice what helps you feel settled and whole, such as certain places, practices or people. Building those into your routine can offer a steady foundation from which to connect with others.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, the Ten of Cups may point to tension or distance in a close group, or to comparing your relationships with an idealized picture. You might ask what each person truly needs to feel at home together. Open, gentle conversations can help rebuild closeness at a realistic pace.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, this card may reflect mutual care, commitment and a shared sense of home, whether with a partner, family, friends or a chosen circle. It can invite you to appreciate the everyday rituals that sustain these bonds. You might express gratitude to the people who make you feel you belong, in words or in small acts.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect a workplace that talks about being a family but does not always act like one, or a blurred line between personal life and work. You might consider which boundaries would protect your time at home. Seeking belonging in several places can ease the pressure on any single one.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect a supportive team, a sense of shared purpose or a workplace where people genuinely care for each other. It may invite you to contribute to that culture. You might notice how feeling valued affects your work, and how you could help others feel the same.

cards.imageryNote: The art gathers ten cups around a group of figures of different ages, sharing an open landscape with a home nearby. Water flowing through green land suggests emotional nourishment that sustains a community. Open arms, linked hands or a shared dance can convey joy and ease. Bright yet gentle colors reflect warmth, safety and the feeling of having arrived somewhere good.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Ten of Cups may reflect harmony that feels strained, or a gap between the picture of a happy home and how things actually feel. You might sense disconnection within a family or group, or feel pressure to maintain an ideal that does not match reality.
It can also point inward: a longing for belonging that is hard to name, or a sense that you have not yet found where you fit.
This card invites you to look at belonging with honesty and compassion. What would feeling at home really look like for you, beyond expectations? You might start with small acts that build closeness, such as sharing a meal or listening without distraction. Belonging often grows slowly, through ordinary moments of care, and it can take many different shapes.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Ten of Cups completes the suit of water with an image of shared happiness: people together in a place that feels like home, with all ten cups gathered around them. It speaks to belonging, emotional fulfillment and the ease of being among people who accept you.
Home in this card is not only a place or a traditional family. It can be chosen family, a close circle of friends, a community or even a moment of peace within yourself. What matters is the feeling of being welcome as you are.
In everyday life, this might look like a relaxed evening with loved ones, a sense of harmony after a difficult period, or simply appreciating the small routines that bind people together. The card invites you to notice where you already feel at home and to nurture those connections. It may also ask what you contribute to that sense of belonging, and how you could share it a little more widely.
cards.name: Ten of Cups
reflectionQuestions: Where, or with whom, do you feel most at home?
What does belonging mean to you, apart from what you were taught it should look like?
What small act could strengthen a sense of home this week?
cards.shortReversed: Harmony may feel strained or out of reach; consider what belonging would mean for you, beyond any ideal picture.
cards.shortUpright: A moment to notice where you already feel at home, and who helps you feel you belong.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask you to be gentle with the more vulnerable parts of yourself. You might notice when you dismiss your own feelings as childish or silly. Offering yourself encouragement, as you would to a young friend, can help sensitivity become a strength rather than something to hide.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Page of Cups invites you to cultivate curiosity about your feelings and hunches. You might keep a notebook for dreams, images or odd impressions, simply to notice patterns over time. Approaching your inner life playfully can make self-understanding feel lighter and more inviting.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to shyness, emotional insecurity or mixed signals in a bond. You might ask whether you or someone close is holding back feelings out of fear of rejection. Gentle honesty, offered at a comfortable pace, can make it easier for both people to feel safe.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Page of Cups may reflect sweet gestures, playful flirting, a heartfelt note or the start of a tender friendship. It can invite you to express affection openly and without overthinking it. You might also notice how someone close shows care in small, surprising ways, and let them know you saw it.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect a creative block, or hesitation to share ideas for fear of criticism. You might try working on something just for yourself first, with no expectation of results. Building confidence slowly can help you bring your ideas forward when they feel ready to be seen.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect a new creative idea, a fresh approach or curiosity about a different area. It may invite you to share an unconventional suggestion or to experiment playfully with a task. Early ideas do not need to be polished; they need room to be explored before anyone judges them.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows a young figure holding a cup at shoulder height, surprised to find a small fish looking back from inside. Their clothes might carry wave or flower patterns, and a shoreline behind them hints at the depths of feeling from which ideas emerge. Soft pastels and a light, curious expression convey openness, imagination and the charm of unexpected messages from within.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Page of Cups may reflect feelings that are hard to share, or creative ideas that feel too fragile to show. You might worry about seeming silly or vulnerable, and keep your inner world tucked away.
It can also point to moods that swing quickly, or to daydreaming that replaces action rather than inspiring it.
This card invites you to treat your sensitive side with patience. What would help you feel safe enough to express yourself, even to one person or on a private page? You might find a low-pressure outlet, like a journal or a sketchbook, where nothing has to be good. If feelings seem big and unsteady, naming them simply can make them easier to hold. Curiosity can grow back once it has a little shelter.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Page of Cups is the youngest figure of the suit of water, often shown gazing at a fish that peeks out of a cup. The image is gently absurd, and that is the point. This card celebrates curiosity, surprise and the willingness to take an unexpected feeling or idea seriously enough to explore it.
It can reflect a new creative impulse, a sudden tenderness toward someone, a hunch that arrives out of nowhere or a playful mood that makes ordinary things feel new. The Page does not need to know where any of this leads. They are simply open.
In daily life, this might look like doodling an idea, writing a heartfelt message, trying a creative hobby or letting yourself be delighted by something small. The card invites you to approach your inner life with the openness of a beginner. You might notice what surprises you today, and give it a moment of attention before practical thoughts crowd in.
cards.name: Page of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What small surprise or idea has caught your attention lately?
How might you share a tender feeling with someone you trust?
What playful creative activity could you try this week, just for the enjoyment of it?
cards.shortReversed: A tender feeling may be hiding or wobbling; consider how you could make it safe to express what you feel.
cards.shortUpright: A playful feeling or a small creative idea may surprise you; this card invites you to meet it with curiosity.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask you to explore the gap between how you imagine yourself and how you act. You might notice a pattern of starting with enthusiasm and then fading. Building gentle routines around your passions can help them last beyond the first rush of feeling.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Knight of Cups invites you to follow what moves you. You might try a creative or compassionate activity simply because it matters to you. Noticing what stirs your heart can clarify your values and help you live by them in ordinary, daily ways.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to mixed messages, moodiness or idealizing someone. You might ask whether feelings are being expressed clearly and consistently, by you and by the other person. Grounding romance in everyday reliability, like keeping small promises, can build deeper trust over time.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Knight of Cups may reflect warmth, romance or a heartfelt gesture, whether with a partner, a friend or someone new. It can invite you to express your feelings sincerely and creatively. You might notice what it feels like to lead with kindness and to let your actions match your words.
aspects.workReversed: Reversed, the card may reflect ideas that stay at the pitching stage, or motivation that rises and falls with your mood. You might break a big vision into smaller steps you can keep. Being honest about your capacity can protect both your ideals and the trust others place in you.
aspects.workUpright: At work, this card can reflect a creative proposal, an idea driven by passion or a role that lets you use your imagination and empathy. It may invite you to pitch something you care about, or to bring more heart to your current tasks. Enthusiasm can be contagious when it is paired with follow-through.

cards.imageryNote: The art shows a rider on a calm horse, moving slowly along a riverbank or through a quiet valley, a cup held forward as an offering. Wave or shell motifs on their armor and cloak can suggest imagination and emotional depth. Flowing water nearby echoes the movement of feeling. Soft blues and silvers, with a touch of warm color, convey romance, sincerity and a dreamy sense of purpose.
cards.meaningReversed:
Reversed, the Knight of Cups may reflect ideals that have drifted away from reality, or feelings that change too quickly to build on. You might notice promises made in a warm moment that are hard to keep, or a tendency to fall for the idea of something more than the thing itself.
It can also turn inward: a creative or romantic impulse that is waiting for more maturity, or a mood that needs understanding before it can guide action.
This card invites you to pair your heart with steadiness. What do you genuinely want, once the glow settles? You might check whether your words and actions line up, and slow down commitments until they feel sustainable. Dreams can stay beautiful while becoming more grounded.
cards.meaningUpright:
The Knight of Cups rides at an unhurried pace, holding a cup out in front as though bringing an offering. Unlike the other knights, this one is not charging ahead. They move through life guided by feelings, ideals and a wish to create beauty or connection.
This card can reflect romance in its broad sense: being moved by people, art, causes or ideas, and wanting to act on that feeling. It may point to an invitation, a creative proposal or a gesture of affection. It can also describe your own ability to follow your heart while still moving forward.
In everyday life, this might look like pursuing a passion project, expressing admiration for someone, or making a choice based on what feels meaningful rather than what is most efficient. The card invites you to honor your ideals and bring them into action with gentleness. You might ask what you would offer the world if you trusted your heart a little more, and what a graceful first step could be.
cards.name: Knight of Cups
reflectionQuestions: What are you drawn toward right now, and what does it say about your values?
Where could your words and actions line up more closely with someone you care about?
What graceful first step could you take toward something that moves you?
cards.shortReversed: Feelings may be running ahead of reality; consider which promises and dreams you can actually carry through.
cards.shortUpright: A heartfelt idea or invitation may be moving toward you; this card invites you to follow what you care about with grace.

aspects.growthReversed: Reversed, this card may ask you to extend compassion toward yourself. You might notice self-criticism that you would never direct at a friend. Gentle routines, rest and boundaries can help you feel steady. If feelings become overwhelming, reaching out to someone you trust can offer support.
aspects.growthUpright: For personal growth, the Queen of Cups invites you to deepen your relationship with your intuition and feelings. You might sit quietly with a question and notice what comes up before you think it through. Practices like journaling or time by water can help you listen inwardly.
aspects.relationshipsReversed: Reversed, this card may point to taking on too much of someone else's emotional weight, or losing sight of your own needs in a bond. You might ask where a gentle boundary could protect both you and the relationship. Caring for yourself can be part of caring for someone else.
aspects.relationshipsUpright: In relationships, the Queen of Cups may reflect deep listening, emotional support and understanding. It can invite you to create a bond where feelings are welcome. You might notice how you offer comfort to others and how you like to receive it, and share that with someone close so care can flow both ways.
